articles.title: Padres closer Mason Miller added to paternity list, will miss pivotal Game 3 on Tuesday vs. Brewers
articles.summary: Miller was tied for third in MLB in saves this year with 38.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres are one game away from elimination, down 2-0 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. They'll be without their All-Star closer as they try to extend their season.

MLB approved a roster change for San Diego, as closer Mason Miller is going on the postseason paternity list and will not be available for Game 3 on Tuesday .

The Padres replaced Miller with reliever Wandy Peralta.

The MLB playoffs come with specific roster rules. A team must submit a roster for each series. If a player is replaced during a series due to injury, he must miss that series and , if the team advances, the following series.

But Miller was added to the postseason paternity list, and there are different rules for that. He can miss a minimum of one day and a maximum of three. When he returns, he can replace Peralta without being forced to sit out another series if San Diego makes a comeback against Milwaukee.

Miller is one of baseball's best closers. He had a career-high 38 saves this season in 66 appearances and finished with a 1.67 ERA.

The 35-year-old Peralta gives the Padres an extra lefty out of the bullpen. He made 65 appearances this season and went 3-3 with a 3.61 ERA.

San Diego heads into Tuesday's Game 3 on the brink of elimination in the best-of-five series. Games 1 and 2 both came down to the wire, with the Brew Crew winning each by one run.

Miller blew the save in Game 2 , when Jackson Chourio laced a walk-off single to center that drove in both Sal Frelick and Christian Yelich, giving Milwaukee a 4-3 victory.

If the Padres lose without Miller on Tuesday, their season is over. If San Diego wins at home Tuesday, the series will continue with Game 4 on Wednesday in San Diego, and Miller would be eligible to return.

articles.title: Dodgers-Braves: Freddie Freeman was booed and robbed of a home run in his return to Atlanta. He got revenge in his next at-bat
articles.summary: Freddie Freeman delivered countless clutch moments for the home team in 12 seasons with the Atlanta Braves. On Tuesday, he delivered one for the visitors.
articles.body:
Freddie Freeman delivered countless clutch moments in the five seasons he played at Truist Park with the Atlanta Braves.

On Tuesday, he delivered one for the visitors after being greeted with boos and being robbed of a home run in Game 3 of the National League Division Series .

With his Los Angeles Dodgers holding a 2-0 lead thanks to a Kiké Hernández home run in the fourth inning, Freeman followed with one of his own two batters later.

With the bases clear and two outs in frame, Braves starter Chris Sale threw a sinker down and inside. Freeman turned on it and sent it clear over the right-field wall.

The solo shot extended the Dodgers' lead to 3-0 and and provided redemption for Freeman after he was robbed of a home run just one inning earlier.

With a man on and no outs in the third, Freeman hit a deep shot off Sale that appeared destined to clear the short fence in left field.

But Mauricio Dubón had a bead on the ball off the bat from his position in left. He leapt in front of the Dodgers' bullpen and corralled the ball before it cleared the fence.

Replay shows that the ball was almost certainly going over the fence had Dubón not gotten there to make the play.

That home-run robbery came on the heels of Freeman being greeted with boos from the Atlanta crowd, who went on to cheer his first-inning strikeout.

But Freeman is a former MVP and three-time World Series champion for a reason. He wasn't fazed by the moment or the hostile Atlanta crowd on Tuesday.

Freeman won his MVP and his first World Series title with the Braves during his 12 seasons with the franchise. Tuesday marked his first playoff game in Atlanta since he left to sign with the Dodgers, whom he has since helped lead to two World Series championships.

There will surely be a chance for Braves fans to celebrate Freeman again after he's retired. But for now, there's no love lost with a trip to the NLCS on the line.

And there's no backing down from Freeman.

articles.title: Dodgers push Braves to the brink of MLB playoff exit
articles.summary: Enrique Hernandez and Freddie Freeman smacked home runs Tuesday to power the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers over Atlanta 3-1 and to the brink of adva...
articles.body:
Enrique Hernandez and Freddie Freeman smacked home runs Tuesday to power the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers over Atlanta 3-1 and to the brink of advancing in the Major League Baseball playoffs.

A two-run blast by Hernandez and a solo shot by former Braves star Freeman in the fourth inning combined with a stellar pitching effort from Japan's Yoshinobu Yamamoto to seal Atlanta's fate.

Yamamoto, a 28-year-old right-hander, struck out 10, matching his MLB career high, while surrendering only one run on four hits over seven innings.

"I was feeling really good. I was able to control my pitches," said Yamamoto through a translator. "That's why I got the swings and misses.

"My fastball was coming out of my hand pretty good so naturally I ended up relying on it."

The Dodgers took a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five National League divisional series, which continues in Atlanta on Wednesday.

The reigning World Series champion Dodgers are trying to win a third consecutive title, something no NL club has ever done.

In a later game, the Milwaukee Brewers seek a road victory at San Diego to complete a sweep of the Padres and reach the best-of-seven NL Championship Series (NLCS) for the second consecutive year.

The Dodgers swept Milwaukee in last year's NLCS.

Yamamoto, last year's World Series Most Valuable Player, improved to 8-1 in his MLB playoff career.

Atlanta ace Chris Sale started against Yamamoto. It was only the third game in MLB playoff history, the first since 1938, with rival starters who both had closed out a World Series-clinching contest.

Sale, a 37-year-old left-hander who threw his first shutout since 2019 in August against the Dodgers, struck out seven while allowing three runs on seven hits over five innings.

After Andy Pages singled to open the fourth, Hernandez smashed a two-run homer over the left-field wall to open the scoring.

Freeman, robbed of a homer by Mauricio Dubon's leaping catch in the third inning, followed moments later with a solo homer for a 3-0 Los Angeles lead.

That gave the Dodgers their first 10 runs of the playoffs all from homers, the longest such streak to start a post-season in MLB history.

Dubon and Lane Thomas opened the Atlanta fifth with back-to-back singles and Yamamoto walked Rowdy Tellez to load the bases.

Drake Baldwin grounded out to first to drive in Dubon from third base but Ronald Acuna grounded out to end the threat.

The Braves threatened in the ninth inning after Ozzie Albies doubled off reliever Edwin Diaz and took third on a Michael Harris ground out.

Dubon then hit a fly out and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to end the game.

Dodgers designated hitter Shohei Ohtani, a four-time MVP who has battled right biceps and left knee injuries, was dropped to fifth in the batting order, his lowest spot in six years.

The Japanese star went 0-for-2 with a walk and a strikeout.

articles.title: Dodgers hit two homers off Chris Sale to steal game three of NLDS behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto
articles.summary: Dave Roberts made a gutsy call turning to Edwin Diaz for the final three outs as the Los Angeles Dodgers clung to a Game 3 lead over Atlanta.

While the Dodgers jumped out to a 5-1 lead thanks to home runs from Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker, and Max Muncy, the Braves battled back in the 9th inning with a two-run homer of their own from Ozzie Albies. It was a sign of things to come in the ensuing games. Game two seemed to set up perfectly for Los Angeles to take command of the series. Instead of using Chris Sale, the Braves decided to give their superstar starter another few days of rest, as they did for much of the regular season. Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez misplayed a fly ball to left field, turning an out into a triple for Michael Harris II. Harris then immediately scored on a wild pitch from reliever Kris Bubic, before doubling in the third run of the game in the 7th inning. Max Muncy homered with the Dodgers down to their last strike to make it 3-2, but Josue De Paula popped up to end it and even the series at a game apiece. That set up a pivotal game three in Atlanta, with Sale now available on regular rest, going against World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Exactly what postseason baseball should be. Sale, who'd obliterated the Dodgers in August, allowing just five hits and striking out 11 in a complete game shutout, looked to be the overwhelming favorite to take down the Dodgers' struggling lefties. But Diaz got out of it, getting Harris to ground out, Dubon flew out in foul territory without allowing the run to score, and Yastrzemski hit a soft grounder to short to end it. articles.title: New Alex Cora Rumors Reveal Managerial Decision for 2027 MLB Season Amid Phillies Buzz
articles.summary: Alex Cora reportedly won't be the next manager of the Philadelphia Phillies.
articles.body:
Alex Cora reportedly won't be the next manager of the Philadelphia Phillies.

According to USA Today's Bob Nightengale , Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski spoke to Cora about becoming the team's new manager. Cora revealed that he's taking the 2027 season off, though.

He was previously offered Philadelphia's manager role in April and declined it to spend the rest of the summer with his family, per Nightengale.

Cora opened the 2026 season as manager of the Boston Red Sox, but was fired after the team started with a disappointing 10-17 record.

The Phillies also made an early manager change during their 2026 campaign, parting ways with Rob Thomson after a 9-13 start to the year.

Don Mattingly served as Philadelphia's interim manager for the remainder of the season, as the team finished with an 88-74 record and made a playoff appearance. The Phillies were ultimately eliminated from the postseason by the Atlanta Braves during their National League Wild Card Series matchup.

Mattingly has expressed interest in remaining Philadelphia's manager beyond the 2026 season, although the team has yet to make a decision regarding his future.

The Phillies' interest in Cora is understandable, as Dombrowski previously spent time with him in Boston from 2018-19.

Cora compiled a 620-541 overall record with the Red Sox, helping them make four postseason appearances in his first seven years as a member of the club. This included a 2018 campaign in which Boston captured its ninth World Series title.

articles.title: Closer Mason Miller hits paternity list 45 minutes before the Padres' season is on the line
articles.summary: Mason Miller lands on MLB's paternity list before a win-or-go-home Game 3, leaving the Padres without their top reliever in an elimination game.
articles.body: San Diego Padres All-Star reliever Mason Miller will miss an elimination game against the Milwaukee Brewers after being placed on Major League Baseball’s paternity list ahead of Game 3 of the National League Division Series. Miller couldn't have picked a worse time to step away, leaving San Diego without its top bullpen weapon right before a win-or-go-home Game 3. The team placed him on the paternity list 45 minutes before the start of the game. articles.title: Yamamoto dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández, Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
articles.summary: Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed only four hits, helping the Los Angeles win 3-1 over Atlanta and take a 2-1 lead in the NL Division Series.
articles.body: ATLANTA — Yoshinobu Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series. Yamamoto dominated the much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Yamamoto, the MVP of the 2025 World Series, permitted only four hits with one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts. His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for the Japanese right-hander. The Dodgers can win the best-of-five series and take another step in their attempt to become the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series titles by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4. The Braves hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth. Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Edwin Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II’s groundout. Díaz stranded the runner when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts. Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn’t be denied an inning later. Hernández’s homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta. Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order. With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher’s interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a fly ball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta’s fourth pitcher. Baldwin’s bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta’s only run. Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain. Tanner Scott added two strikeouts in a scoreless eighth for Los Angeles. Up next Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.

articles.title: Brewers manager Pat Murphy declines to censor himself as things go badly during in-game interview that's actually worth hearing
articles.summary: In-game interviews are generally worthless. Here's the exception.
articles.body:
In-game interviews are generally worthless. This is the exception.

With the San Diego Padres and Brewers locked in a scoreless tie early in Tuesday's NLDS Game 3 — a 4-3 Padres win that extended the series — Milwaukee's Sal Frelick hit a line drive to center field at Petco Park.

The ball was well-struck and looked like extra bases if it landed. But Padres center fielder Jackson Merrill had the ball in his sights off the bat.

This all happened as Brewers manager Pat Murphy conducted an interview with FS1 sideline reporter Tom Verducci. Verducci asked Murphy how he liked the approach of his team up to that point in the game. As Murphy started to answer, Frelick hit his line drive.

Here's Murphy's response, which swiftly shifts as he realizes the ball is doomed for Merrill's glove:

"Eh, we've been a little antsy, I think we've swang at some pitches … Get in the gap, Sal! God damn it, Merrill!"

The broadcast quickly pivoted back to the booth team of Adam Amin, Adam Wainwright and A.J. Pierzynski, who shared a few chuckles at what they and the entire broadcast audience had just witnessed. The production crew then deftly zoomed in to a closeup of Murphy looking on sternly at the game from the Milwaukee dugout.

It added up to a few moments of baseball broadcast gold. In a sports broadcast world littered with terrible in-game interviews, few, if any, have been better than this.

articles.title: Dodgers grind down Chris Sale as Braves' offensive woes continue in NLDS Game 3 loss
articles.summary: Any one of the Braves' big hitters could've tied this game with a timely swing. The problem is they didn't.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — In the middle of every fifth inning at home, the Braves roll out a promotion in which a fan races "The Freeze," a sprinter in an ice-blue bodysuit. The fan gets a head start to run around the perimeter of the outfield, but soon enough, the Freeze starts hunting. On Tuesday, a fan in a Ronald Acuña Jr. jersey outran The Freeze for a surprisingly long distance … but eventually face-planted on the warning-track dirt just as The Freeze cruised past him to victory.

As metaphors for the Braves' 3-1 NLDS Game 3 loss to the Dodgers go, it was pretty on the nose. With everything set up in its favor — a split on the road, ace on the hill, full home stadium on a perfect, 74-degree night — Atlanta slipped just once and was lost.

Diagnosing what went wrong in this game for the Braves, who now face elimination on Wednesday, isn't hard. Starter Chris Sale made, by his estimation, two bad pitches, both of which ended up in the Truist Park seats. The Braves' key hitters weren't able to match the Dodgers' fireworks, perpetuating a run of ice-cold hitting that's now threatening to end their season.

"We've just got to get some key hits in key moments and get guys comfortable. It's as simple as that," Austin Riley said after the game in a quiet Braves locker room. "We had some opportunities tonight and just didn't get it done."

Sale, fresh off a dominant bookend performance in the wild-card series victory over Philadelphia, took the mound on full rest on Tuesday. And while he struck out seven over five innings, he had to go deep into the count on virtually every batter.

"They did a nice job of really grinding the at-bats and passing the baton," Braves manager Walt Weiss said postgame. "He had to work hard. He had to work hard to get the outs that he got."

You see that many pitches, and you start to pick out some favorites, and by the fourth inning, the Dodgers did exactly that. Kiké Hernández rifled a 92-mph inside changeup 406 feet, scoring Andy Pages. Two batters later, Freddie Freeman turned on an inside sinker to put the score at 3-0 — a Dodgers run total that would hold up the rest of the game.

"One bad inning ruined the whole game," Sale said. "Yanked a changeup to Kiké. We all know what he can do in October when the lights are bright. Actually made a pretty good pitch to Freddie, but he was either looking for it or saw it out of the hand."

One inning later, with 95 pitches in the books, Sale was cashed. "Getting Chris Sale out of the game after five innings," Freeman said later, "is a huge win no matter what the score is."

The Braves probably could've weathered a subpar — by Sale's standards — outing from their ace. But the vibes were off all game for Atlanta, both in the field and in the stands. The fans made the wrong choice in the cap shuffle game. The stadium PA tried to fire up the fans with "make some noise!" blasts, which really shouldn't be necessary in October. And, of course, there was the guy in the Acuña jersey walking away from his race against The Freeze with nothing but a mouthful of dirt.

That guy was only mirroring the struggles of the real Acuña, who's now 3-for-21 — with three singles — in this postseason. In Game 3, he had his moment teed up — the bottom of the fifth, two men on, down 3-1 — but Acuña could only ground out, killing the Braves' best scoring chance of the night.

An Ozzie Albies double to start the ninth gave the Braves one last chance at late heroics, with the tying run at the plate and no outs. But three batters later, Atlanta was done. And the questions about the Braves' offensive whimpering only gained strength.

Afterward, Weiss pushed back on the idea that Acuña, Drake Baldwin (3-for-23, six strikeouts this postseason) and Matt Olson (4-for-23, 1 homer, 9 strikeouts) are mired in unbreakable slumps.

"Those guys have been our aircraft carriers all year," he said. "Every time one of those guys steps in the box, I think something good is going to happen. Those guys, they're always one at-bat away from changing a game."

He's right. The Dodgers are relentless, yes, but also beatable. Any one of the Braves' big hitters could have tied this game — or won it — with a timely swing. The problem is they didn't, and now there aren't that many at-bats left for the Braves to salvage their season.

"We've had our back against the wall before," Sale said. "We're a resilient group. We have confidence in ourselves and each other. So, yeah, we'll take this one off the chin and show up [Wednesday] ready to win a game."

Braves fans (and the tight surrounding buildings) can make Truist Park one of the loudest in baseball, but the fans are also a trailing indicator of the team's performance; they need to see some results before they truly commit to cheering. (One of the loudest spontaneous reactions of the night: the boos for Freeman, a former hometown hero . Nothing but love between Freddie and the Atlanta fans, but this is October.)

With grinding patience, Los Angeles was able to take Sale out of the game and the fight out of the crowd on Tuesday, and neither the Braves nor their fans could get up off the deck. Now everyone in a Braves uniform — both on the field and in the stands — will have one more chance to extend this season, one more chance to avoid an offseason of second-guessing and what-could-have-been.

articles.title: Yoshinobu Yamamoto adds to his already sterling postseason résumé, puts the Dodgers back in control in NLDS Game 3: 'He's just not afraid'
articles.summary: Yamamoto delivered 7 innings of 1-run ball as the Dodgers took a 2-1 series lead in Atlanta.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Will Smith couldn't make out exactly what Yoshinobu Yamamoto was saying.

Perhaps it was the language barrier. The Dodgers had already made a mound visit in the fifth inning, meaning interpreter Will Ireton could not reemerge from the dugout. And so, only Smith and third baseman Kiké Hernández, a close confidant of Yamamoto's, joined the all-world hurler on the hill.

Or maybe Yamamoto was drowned out by the Truist Park crowd, rising, chanting, chopping, glad to finally be in the presence of something worth cheering for.

Because after four innings of calm dominance, Yamamoto, October's sharpest buzzsaw, looked to be on the ropes in NLDS Game 3 .

Atlanta's offense, down 3-0 in the fifth, had juiced the bases with one out. As Yamamoto, Smith and Hernández congregated on the mound, Drake Baldwin, leadoff hitter and All-Star, lurked ominously in the left-handed batter's box. Darude's "Sandstorm" jumped from the ballpark speakers. A moment, the kind that makes playoff baseball a special beast, was building.

The Braves had found themselves in possession of something rare, something precious, something worth seizing: a postseason opportunity against one of the greats. For the first time all season, Yamamoto was unmoored enough to require two mound visits in the same inning.

But Hernández, as he has been so often for the Dodgers over the years, was in the right place at the right time.

"[I went to the mound] because of the relationship with Yoshi and what we've gone through together," Hernández told Yahoo Sports after Los Angeles' 3-1 win on Tuesday . "I'm glad I was there."

The L.A. stalwart and cult hero, whose fourth-inning, two-run blast (his 17th career postseason homer) had gotten the scoring started, understood what Yamamoto was trying to convey and knew how to communicate it to Smith.

"I was able to translate because of my good Japanese," he added in jest.

"That was an encouraging moment," Yamamoto acknowledged afterward. "He told me just be yourself, even though that was a little bit like a dirty word."

The Braves, after failing to take advantage, likely uttered a cuss or two themselves.

Baldwin grounded out meekly to first, driving in Atlanta's first run in the process. That brought the slumping Ronald Acuña Jr. to the dish with the chance for a signature October highlight. Instead, the 2023 NL MVP bounced an inning-ending, rally-burning, game-killing, potentially season-altering grounder to second baseman Miguel Rojas. The threat was quelled, the window was closed. The reigning World Series MVP, and his three-peat-seeking ballclub, were back in control.

Yamamoto set down the next six hitters he faced, breezily tossing up zeros in the sixth and seventh frames before giving way to Los Angeles' bullpen. In all, it was yet another sensational October outing by the diminutive right-hander: 7 innings, 1 run, 10 strikeouts.

"Wow. What a performance," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts gushed postgame. "... He just has a way to just make pitches, calm his heartbeat."

So much of the conversation entering Tuesday's crucial contest centered on Braves ace Chris Sale, who, after Atlanta's surprise Game 2 victory , had a chance to push the Dodgers to the brink. But the Dodgers ground Sale down in the early going , working up his pitch count and setting the stage for Hernández's big swing in the fourth. Sale was done after five.

Yamamoto, on the other hand, went seven innings in a playoff game for the third time since he came over from Japan ahead of 2024. The only other player to accomplish that in the same span? Dodgers Game 1 starter Tarik Skubal.

"He's just not afraid," catcher Will Smith said of Yamamoto.

And while Yamamoto's secured eternal-hero status with that Game 7, no-rest, World Series relief appearance for the ages, the totality of his postseason résumé is similarly impressive, historic, awe-inspiring.

After Tuesday's gem, Yamamoto holds the second-lowest postseason career ERA in MLB history among pitchers with at least 10 postseason starts. The only name ahead of him, San Francisco Giants icon Madison Bumgarner, is well within reach, with a 2.11 to Yamamoto's 2.14. And the Dodgers' ace, almost certainly, should have many, many more chances to shrink that number. He's still just 28 years old, and Los Angeles is in the playoffs every year.

The legend is already large, yet the legend is still building.

Somehow, the same can be said for Hernández, who at 35 years old, was not guaranteed to be part of this year's Dodgers story. After playing a key role in last year's epic Game 7 alongside Yamamoto, Hernández hit the free-agent market. A return to L.A. was far from certain. He hadn't been a league-average hitter since the 2021 season. Age and injuries were starting to pile up.

Then he re-signed with the Dodgers late in the offseason, after pitchers and catchers had reported, but appeared in just 41 games. His health and his place on this October roster were never a given.

Yet in some ways, this was also inevitable.

Amidst Los Angeles' financial might and player development prowess and institutional grandeur, Hernández represents a more human side of this juggernaut. If Yamamoto, alongside Shohei Ohtani, is a cornerstone of this glorious Dodgers run and all it represents, Hernández is an appreciated connection to a bygone era, a holdover with a clutch gene.

This mercurial goofball has been a fundamental part of this organization's DNA for the better part of the past decade. He is a flawed ballplayer, in a year-over-year decline. He is also indispensable. After not playing in the first two games of this series, Hérnandez delivered the biggest swing of its third. And nobody was particularly surprised. All those experiences in big moments allow Hernández to be thoroughly unperturbed by the scale of it all. None of this feels big to him anymore, even if it still does to the rest of us.

"I don't know how much it means," Hernández responded to a reporter's question about what the home run meant to him. "But it feels good."

So do the Dodgers, back where they believe they belong, with a 2-1 series lead, thanks to these two dissimilar postseason pillars.

articles.title: Padres Beat Brewers to Avoid Elimination, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The San Diego Padres aren't done yet.
articles.body:
San Diego defeated the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 in Tuesday's Game 3 of their National League Division series at Petco Park. Milwaukee still leads the series 2-1, but the Padres now have momentum thanks to timely hitting and clutch pitching.

Jake Cronenworth launched a homer, Manny Machado and Fernando Tatis Jr. each notched an RBI, and the shorthanded bullpen got the job done to preserve the season.

A return home was an opportunity for the Padres to put two shocking losses behind them and work toward a potential comeback. It seemed as if they were going to take the lead in the ninth inning of Game 1 when Ty France launched a deep fly ball with a man on base that may have cleared the fence, but it hit the roof and fell into Jackson Chourio's glove for an out.

As if that wasn't difficult enough, San Diego had the lead in the bottom of the ninth in Game 2 just for star closer Mason Miller to blow a save.

A quick start to move on seemed paramount, and the home team got just that thanks to small ball in the third inning. Samad Taylor singled, stole a base, advanced on a bunt and scored on Tatis' RBI ground out before Jackson Merrill singled, stole a base and scored on Machado's RBI single.

Milwaukee chased Padres starter Nick Pivetta from the game after 4.1 innings with William Contreras cutting the deficit in half with a solo homer and Chourio tying it with a sacrifice fly that featured aggressive base running from Cooper Pratt.

With Brewers starter Dustin May already unable to record an out past the third, it was a bullpen game the rest of the way. Bullpen games typically favor the Padres on paper, but they were without Miller because he was placed on the paternity list.

Unlike the first two games, it was San Diego that responded in the pressure-packed moments Tuesday.

Cronenworth broke the tie with a solo homer in the fifth, while Xander Bogaerts provided some breathing room when he singled, advanced on a wild pitch and scored on a throwing error from Pratt in the sixth.

Still, putting away the Brewers is never easy. Bradgley Rodriguez escaped with runners on second and third in the sixth, but he gave up an RBI single to Christian Yelich in the seventh before striking out Garrett Mitchell to avoid more damage.

With Miller unavailable and questions looming about Adrian Morejon's availability, San Diego turned to Game 2 starter Michael King in a stunning development.

All he did was pitch a scoreless eighth and remain in the game to close the door in the ninth by inducing a double play from Yelich.

articles.title: Padres closer Mason Miller misses Game 3 win over Brewers after being added to paternity list
articles.summary: Mason Miller was tied for third in MLB in saves this year with 38.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres found a way to extend their season without All-Star closer Mason Miller.

The Padres climbed back into the NLDS and beat the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Tuesday at Petco Park. That gave them their first win in the series and forced Game 4 on Wednesday.

And they did it all without their star closer.

MLB approved a roster change for San Diego on Tuesday afternoon, as Miller landed on the postseason paternity list. Miller's wife, who was due to give birth to the couple's first child later this month, went into labor Tuesday afternoon. As a result, the All-Star was not available for Game 3. The Padres replaced him with reliever Wandy Peralta.

The MLB playoffs come with specific roster rules. A team must submit a roster for each series. If a player is replaced during a series due to injury, he must miss that series and , if the team advances, the following series.

But Miller was added to the postseason paternity list, and there are different rules for that. He can miss a minimum of one day and a maximum of three. When he returns, he can replace Peralta without being forced to sit out another series.

Miller is one of baseball's best closers. He had a career-high 38 saves this season in 66 appearances and finished with a 1.67 ERA.

The 35-year-old Peralta gives the Padres an extra lefty out of the bullpen. He made 65 appearances this season and went 3-3 with a 3.61 ERA.

San Diego is still on the brink of elimination in the best-of-five series. Games 1 and 2 both came down to the wire, with the Brew Crew winning each by one run.

Miller blew the save in Game 2 , when Jackson Chourio laced a walk-off single to center that drove in both Sal Frelick and Christian Yelich, giving Milwaukee a 4-3 victory.

After the Padres' win at home on Tuesday, the series continues with Game 4 on Wednesday in San Diego. Miller is eligible to return for that contest. Whether he'll be ready to do so remains to be seen.

articles.title: Padres avoid elimination after 4-3 win over Brewers in NLDS Game 3
articles.summary: Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night.
articles.body: SAN DIEGO — Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night. Xander Bogaerts turned a game-ending double play at shortstop for the Padres, who trimmed Milwaukee’s lead in the best-of-five series to 2-1 with a tense, back-and-forth victory over the MLB-best Brewers. Game 4 is Wednesday night at Petco Park. If necessary, Game 5 will be back in Milwaukee on Friday. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado drove in early runs for the Padres, but their bullpen didn’t have star closer Mason Miller, who went on the paternity list about 45 minutes before the first pitch. King stepped up after pitching five innings just two days ago and finished it off — but only after a thrilling ninth. The right-hander retired four of his first five batters, but William Contreras and Brice Turang drew one-out walks in the ninth. Christian Yelich then cracked a 107 mph line drive up the middle, where Bogaerts went down to his knees to field it on a short hop and scampered to touch second base before throwing out Yelich at first to end it. King earned his first save since 2023, his first in the postseason and his first for the Padres. Contreras homered and had three hits for the Brewers, who lost their 12th consecutive postseason road game dating to the 2018 National League Championship Series. Yelich even got his first playoff RBI since 2018 with a seventh-inning single, but Milwaukee fell behind early and never led, leaving 11 runners on base. Padres back on track The Padres had won 19 of 22 and swept the Cubs out of the Wild Card Series before losing two straight heartbreakers in Milwaukee last weekend, but they are fighting to stay with the majors’ best regular-season team. The clubs have played three consecutive one-run games in this NLDS, all decided by late-game execution — and this time, the Padres came through. They were also bailed out by King, largely a reliever early in his major league career with the Yankees. This game was just his third relief appearance in three seasons with San Diego — and according to OptaStats, he is the first pitcher to start a postseason game and then earn a two-inning save within the next two days since saves became an official statistic in 1969. Back-and-forth game Neither starter excelled on a tense, uncommonly hot October night in downtown San Diego. Nick Pivetta yielded two runs and five hits while pitching into the fifth for the Padres, and Dustin May got pulled abruptly with a 1-0 count on Bogaerts and a runner on in the fourth. Samad Taylor and Jackson Merrill put San Diego ahead in the third when both singled, stole second and scored. Contreras answered with his second homer of the series, adding a theatrical trot around the bases. Cooper Pratt tied it right after Pivetta’s exit when Dustin Harris couldn’t throw him out on Jackson Chourio’s 242-foot sacrifice fly. It was the fifth RBI of the series for the 22-year-old Chourio and his 16th in 15 career postseason games, already tying Ryan Braun for the franchise record. Cronenworth lined JoJo Romero’s first pitch of the fifth over the wall in right for only his second hit of the postseason. Bogaerts then singled in the sixth, advanced on a wild pitch and scored when Pratt bounced his throw from shortstop for an error after Miguel Andujar’s broken bat came flying toward him along with the grounder. San Diego’s outfield couldn’t get to Turang’s bloop single with two outs in the seventh, and Yelich singled home Contreras for his first playoff RBI since he homered in Game 7 of the 2018 NLCS against the Dodgers — a span of 87 plate appearances over 19 games. Up next Neither team had announced its Game 4 starter.

articles.title: Predicting the Outcome for Each MLB Team's Top 2026-27 Free Agent
articles.summary: The 2026-27 MLB offseason is marked by uncertainty, as the expiring CBA and expected lockout threaten to derail the hot stove and free agency until the situation is sorted out.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 MLB offseason is marked by uncertainty, as the expiring CBA and expected lockout threaten to derail the hot stove and free agency until the situation is sorted out.

It is a relatively thin free-agent market this winter, anchored by one true superstar in Tarik Skubal, but there is plenty of secondary talent that can help reshape a contender's roster.

Ahead, we've highlighted each team's top upcoming free agent and made our best guess on whether they will re-sign with their current club or wind up elsewhere this offseason.

Baltimore Orioles: SP Trevor Rogers (Age: 28)

One of the few no-doubt qualifying offer candidates on the market this winter, Rogers had a 4.03 ERA, 1.19 WHIP and 157 strikeouts in 169.2 innings. Given the glaring need for starting pitching, the O's can't afford to lose arguably their best arm, so re-signing him should be a top priority.

Gray is a lock to decline his end of a $30 million mutual option in favor of a $10 million buyout. After going 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP and 149 strikeouts in 169.0 innings, he should have no problem finding more guaranteed money. A healthy Garrett Crochet can replace him atop the Red Sox rotation, with Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello behind him.

New York Yankees: RP David Bednar (Age: 31)

Jazz Chisholm Jr. (137 G, 97 OPS+, 1.7 WAR) and Trent Grisham (121 G, 95 OPS+, 0.6 WAR) were the top upcoming free agents on the Yankees roster entering the season, but both had down years. Instead, Bednar (64 G, 35 SV, 2.47 ERA, 9.9 K/9) looks like the most impactful potential departure. He would be difficult to replace at the back of the Yankees bullpen.

Tampa Bay Rays: SP Nick Martinez (Age: 36)

Freddy Peralta probably ends up landing the bigger contract given his age and track record, but Martinez is the team's top free agent based on this year's production. The 36-year-old went 15-6 with a 3.10 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 109 strikeouts in 180.0 innings, and both ends of his $20 million mutual option might get declined given Tampa Bay's financial limitations. The Rays don't pay for a career year at 36. They look for the next candidate to deliver one.

Toronto Blue Jays: SP Shane Bieber (Age: 31)

Forearm fatigue sidelined Bieber until June 23. He made just 11 starts before shoulder inflammation ended his season at the end of August, but he had a 2.59 ERA over 24.1 innings in his final four starts before hitting the shelf. At 31 years old, he represents a quality buy-low target, but the Blue Jays might be hunting for more stability as they rebuild their staff.

Chicago White Sox: RP Sean Newcomb (Age: 33)

There was some talk of Newcomb returning to a starting role after the White Sox signed him to a one-year, $4.5 million deal, but he has instead been one of their top relievers. He recorded more than three outs in 39 of his 60 appearances, posting a 3.09 ERA in 90.1 innings. His ability to chew up innings and fill multiple roles on the staff is valuable enough for the White Sox to prioritize bringing him back, even if his price tag jumps.

Cleveland Guardians: SP Foster Griffin (Age: 31)

After three years in the Japanese League, Griffin went 12-3 with a 3.06 ERA in 129.1 innings with the Nationals before he was traded to the Guardians at the deadline in exchange for four prospects. He had a 5.19 ERA in nine starts after coming to Cleveland. With Gavin Williams, Parker Messick, Tanner Bibee and Joey Cantillo returning to anchor the staff, he is a safe bet to depart.

Detroit Tigers: 2B Gleyber Torres (Age: 29)

Torres tallied 5.0 WAR in 241 games in Detroit. He returned on a qualifying offer last winter, but the club has potential in-house replacements this time around. Hao-Yu Lee (114 G, 107 OPS+, 31 XBH, 1.0 WAR) put together a strong rookie season, while Max Anderson (108 G, .302 BA, .863 OPS at Triple-A) is knocking on the door. Plugging them in at second base would allow the front office to focus on rebuilding the rotation.

Kansas City Royals: IF Jonathan India (Age: 29)

India played just 17 games before undergoing season-ending shoulder surgery. It has been a nagging issue throughout his career. He had a 105 OPS+ and 1.7 WAR in 151 games during his final season with the Reds in 2024. While he will likely have to settle for a minor league deal, his age and versatility will help drive interest.

Minnesota Twins: C Ryan Jeffers (Age: 29)

The Twins held on to Jeffers at the trade deadline. He posted a 127 OPS+ with 35 extra-base hits, 14 home runs and 2.8 WAR as one of the most productive backstops in baseball. The Twins used the No. 3 overall pick in the 2026 draft on catcher Vahn Lackey. He is expected to move quickly through the minors, but Jeffers could be the perfect veteran bridge on a two- or three-year deal.

With Shea Langeliers limited by a knee injury, Heim was acquired from the Braves for cash considerations in May. He ended up starting 58 games behind the plate for the Athletics, hitting .201/.255/.361 with 15 doubles, 12 home runs and 35 RBI in 345 plate appearances. The former All-Star and Gold Glove winner will have a better chance at playing time elsewhere in 2027 with Langeliers back healthy.

Houston Astros: RP Bryan Abreu (Age: 29)

Even in what was statistically the worst season of his career, Abreu still posted a 3.73 ERA with nine saves and 16 holds in 66 appearances. His 29.9 percent strikeout rate was still elite, but it was accompanied by a 15.3 percent walk rate. A multi-year deal awaits from a contender confident it can dial in his command, while Miguel Ullola gives Houston a potential replacement in high-leverage spots.

Los Angeles Angels: IF Adam Frazier (Age: 34)

The Angels are thin on notable free agents, with veterans Travis d'Arnaud and Yoán Moncada coming off seasons where they were a non-factor. Frazier at least still had a little something in the tank, posting a .240/.315/.349 line and 0.4 WAR in 66 games after signing a minor league deal.

Seattle Mariners: OF Randy Arozarena (Age: 31)

Arozarena is one of the few players on the market capable of reeling in a $100 million payday. That will push Seattle's financial limits, but can they afford to let him walk? The Mariners were 28th in the majors in runs scored. Arozarena led the team in OPS+ (148), hits (161), home runs (26), RBI (79), and WAR (5.7). Pay the man!

Texas Rangers: RP Tyler Alexander (Age: 32)

The Rangers did an excellent job assembling a quality bullpen. Alexander was a significant piece of the puzzle after inking a one-year, $1.125 million deal. The southpaw logged a 3.70 ERA with four saves and 14 holds in 75 appearances. His 49.5 percent groundball rate was a career high as he leaned more heavily on his sinker and changeup. His career renaissance should create some mutual interest in a reunion.

Atlanta Braves: SP Tyler Mahle (Age: 32)

Mahle was as impactful as any deadline pickup, posting a 1.99 ERA and 0.96 WHIP in 54.1 innings over nine starts after he was acquired from the Giants. Then, he tossed seven strong innings against the Phillies in the Wild Card Series. Even if Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach are back next year, Mahle would be a great stabilizing presence in the rotation.

Closer Pete Fairbanks is expected to miss a significant portion of the 2027 season recovering from thoracic outlet surgery. He struggled to a 6.31 ERA in 41.1 innings before his season ended prematurely. He is the only departing free agent on the Miami roster. Fairbanks will likely need to throw for scouts and prove he's healthy before landing a new contract.

The Mets did a good job offloading their upcoming free agents at the deadline, leaving Bo Bichette's future as the only real discussion point in the departing free agent conversation. Given his lackluster season, the expectation is that Bichette will opt into his $42 million salary for 2027, knowing he can opt out again next winter ahead of the final year of his deal.

Arraez hit .310/.346/.419 for a 113 OPS+ while also proving he can play a capable second base (1,275.1 INN, -4 DRS, 12 OAA), which significantly limited his market a year ago. Alec Bohm and Edmundo Sosa are also free agents, so the Phillies have some decisions to make retooling their infield, but a third baseman or outfielder is a cleaner roster fit if they spend on a bat.

The Nationals released Miles Mikolas and Trevor Williams in August, leaving the roster without any notable free agents. The only players on the books for the 2027 season are Keibert Ruiz and Cade Cavalli, giving the Nationals significant flexibility in building next year's roster, but there are no decisions to make regarding in-house free agents.

No team has more outgoing talent than the Cubs, with Suzuki, Ian Happ, Michael Conforto and Tyrone Taylor all potentially leaving from the outfield contingent, while the entire starting rotation of Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Matthew Boyd (mutual option) and Clay Holmes (player option) is also potentially out the door.

With a 131 OPS+ and 26 home runs in a 5.1-WAR season, Suzuki looks like the hardest to replace, given the lack of impact bats on the market. Expect a reunion with one of Suzuki or Happ, although both players could stay if Happ is willing to offer up a discount to stick around.

Cincinnati Reds: C Tyler Stephenson (Age: 30)

Stephenson has averaged 18 home runs and 73 RBI per 162 games during his time in the big leagues. He logged a 101 OPS+ with 22 doubles, 15 home runs and 54 RBI in a 2.5-WAR season in 2026. The Reds can go with Jose Trevino as the primary catcher next season, ideally bridging the gap until top prospect Alfredo Duno arrives.

Milwaukee Brewers: 1B Jake Bauers (Age: 31)

With a modest $2.7 million salary in 2026, Bauers produced a 140 OPS+ with 22 doubles, 26 home runs, 86 RBI and 3.3 WAR in the middle of the Milwaukee lineup. That production will be tough to replace, but after carrying a payroll under $150 million this season, the Brewers will likely let someone else pay for his career year.

Pittsburgh Pirates: 2B Brandon Lowe (Age: 32)

The good news is that the Pirates are starting to spend. They handed out the largest free agency deal in franchise history last winter. The bad news is that record-setting deal was a two-year, $29 million contract for Ryan O'Hearn. It's likely going to cost $20 million annually and at least three years to re-sign Lowe, but he was instrumental in the club's offensive turnaround, posting a 121 OPS+ with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and 5.4 WAR. There is reportedly mutual interest in a reunion, but it will take uncharted spending.

The Cardinals traded away Dustin May and JoJo Romero at the deadline, leaving the roster without a notable upcoming free agent. They do have a $6 million club option on reliever Ryne Stanek, which will likely be declined as the club continues to focus on building for the future.

Arizona Diamondbacks: SP Michael Soroka (Age: 29)

Given his age and 2026 production (21 GS, 3.41 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 114 K, 116.0 IP), Soroka quietly pitched his way to being one of the better second-tier starters on the market this winter. That should make declining his end of a $10 million mutual option an easy decision. While the D-backs have every reason to pursue a reunion, there will be significant interest elsewhere from contenders.

Colorado Rockies: SP Kyle Freeland (Age: 33)

Freeland has spent his entire 10-year career with the Rockies. He leads the franchise in starts (257), innings pitched (1,395.2) and pitching WAR (18.9). He served up a 6.69 ERA in 135.1 innings in 2026, backed by a slightly less terrible 5.09 FIP. The Rockies need innings badly enough to pursue a reunion and hope for a bounce back.

Los Angeles Dodgers: SP Tarik Skubal (Age: 29)

With a price tag expected to push toward $400 million, there is a finite number of teams capable of signing Skubal. The Dodgers are right at the top of that list. The Mets have the money and the need, but another year of irrelevance won't make it any easier to attract elite talent. The imminent lockout and new CBA are obviously a major unknown, but for now the Dodgers have to be viewed as the favorites to lock up the two-time Cy Young winner.

San Diego Padres: SP Michael King (Age: 31)

King can opt out of the final two years and $58 million of his contract this winter. He almost certainly will since he would immediately slot in as the No. 2 starter on the market behind Tarik Skubal. The Padres also have Adrian Morejón, Ty France, Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Jason Adam as free agents, so they will have multiple roster holes to fill, but retaining King as the staff ace should be their top priority.

San Francisco Giants: RP JT Brubaker (Age: 32)

Brubaker made 52 starts for the Pirates in 2021 and 2022 before arm issues derailed his career, but he returned as a solid bullpen arm for the Giants this year, logging a 3.58 ERA in 60.1 innings over 41 appearances. It will be interesting to see if he gets any nibbles as a low-cost rotation candidate this offseason. He will likely test the open market.

articles.title: They were a historically bad team. Now they’re a threat to make the World Series.
articles.summary: The Chicago White Sox are up 2-0 in the American League Division Series, a shocking turnaround after three straight 100-loss seasons.
articles.body: CHICAGO — Many Chicago White Sox fans were genuinely cheering for the team to lose just two years ago. In late September 2024, the White Sox were taking the field for their final home series of the season. The attendance was sparse, but those who did show up were hoping to witness history, as Chicago was one defeat away from setting the record for losses in a 162-game season. The White Sox, of course, let them down, winning their final three home games before they lost their record 121st game on the road in their next series. Fast-forward to today, and the unthinkable has happened: The White Sox are returning home as heroes. Chicago will play its first playoff game at home since 2021 on Wednesday. And the White Sox will enter their matchup with the Cleveland Guardians up 2-0 in the American League Division Series, one win away from advancing to the Championship Series. The five years between home playoff games were not kind to fans of the South Siders. After a respectable 81-81 finish in 2022, Chicago nosedived. The White Sox lost 101 games in 2023, 121 in 2024 and 102 more last year. This season, they became the first team to make the playoffs after back-to-back 100-loss seasons — which also means they’re the first team to do so after three straight 100-loss seasons. On Wednesday, the Sox will have another chance at history, as they haven’t clinched a playoff series in front of their home fans since 1906. The fans have been “waiting 120 years, so maybe we can do it this year,” pitcher Grant Taylor, who recorded saves in each of the first two wins against the Guardians, told reporters Monday. “I think it’s going to be unbelievable. Those fans deserve it. They’ve been with us for three years of 100 losses, and they’ve been with us a good bit this year giving us a lot of support as we’ve gone through this. So being able to give them a postseason game is going to be pretty special.” Chicago has turned over most of its team since the 2024 season. Only four hitters and five players were on the roster then and now, per MLB.com. The White Sox have improved through several avenues since. In the offseason, they signed Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami. Murakami, 26, blasted 35 homers in his first MLB regular season, and he has added one more through his first four playoff appearances. (Murakami also captured the attention of fans thanks to his enthusiastic postgame interviews.) Meanwhile, pitchers such as Taylor and starter Sean Burke have emerged after having been drafted years ago. Taylor had a 2.25 ERA in 84 innings during the regular season. Burke struck out 185 batters across 32 appearances (including 27 starts) and finished 17th among all pitchers in wins above replacement. In addition to an explosive offense that was top 10 in both home runs and slugging percentage during the regular season, the White Sox have employed a unique pitching strategy, relying heavily on their relievers to throw multiple innings. “We knew we had to be different,” general manager Chris Getz told MLB Network this month. “It became leaning into those arms. What’s the pathway to win? How do we solve today? Oftentimes it was getting creative with openers. Thankfully, we’ve got some arms that can go multiple innings.” (It’s also possible the team’s success is coming from a higher power, as Pope Leo XIV is a fan. “I willingly invoke the Almighty’s abundant blessings upon you and your loved ones,” the pope wrote in a letter to the team in September.) The man in charge of the dugout is Will Venable, who played in the majors from 2008 to 2016. Venable became Chicago’s manager in October 2024 and has become a key part of the franchise’s turnaround. “For where the organization was and the pain of those couple years in which there was 100-loss seasons, to see the growth and have the fans be a part of this and be able to celebrate this, it makes me happy for everyone involved with White Sox baseball,” Venable said after the White Sox won in the wild-card round. As impressive as the revival has been so far, the Sox don’t seem simply happy to be here. Asked in September what Chicago could do in the playoffs, designated hitter Andrew Benintendi told MLB.com his team was “confident.” Added Benintendi: “We are dumb enough to think we can win it. So, why not?”

articles.title: Dodgers' Yoshinobu Yamamoto Makes MLB History With Rare Stat After NLDS Win vs. Braves
articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers starting pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto's impressive run of postseason dominance continued Tuesday in a 3-1 road win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers starting pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto's impressive run of postseason dominance continued Tuesday in a 3-1 road win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series.

According to OptaStats, Yamamoto became the first pitcher in MLB history to earn a win, while also allowing one or fewer runs and one or fewer walks in five consecutive playoff appearances:

Predicting the Outcome for Each MLB Team's Top 2026-27 Free Agent

Yamamoto was a dominant force once again Tuesday, allowing just four hits and one run, while walking one and striking out 10 over seven innings.

The Japanese ace's lone blemish came in the fifth inning when Mauricio Dubón scored on an RBI groundout by Braves catcher Drake Baldwin.

Yamamoto, 28, signed a 12-year, $325 million dollar contract with the Dodgers in December 2023 after starring overseas for several years, and he has proved to be worth the investment.

He won the World Series in each of his first two MLB seasons, while also being named World Series MVP last year.

Since giving up five runs in his first career playoff start, Yamamoto has only given up more than one run in two of his past 10 playoff outings, and he has not allowed more than three runs during that span.

In last year's tightly contested World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays, Yamamoto earned three wins over two starts and one relief appearance, collectively giving up just 10 hits and two earned runs in 17.2 innings pitched.

That form has carried over to the 2026 postseason, and it came at the perfect time for the Dodgers.

After beating the Braves in Game 1, L.A. lost Game 2 of the NLDS despite having a huge pitching advantage with Blake Snell facing an opener.

That win gave Atlanta a ton of momentum, especially given the knowledge that their ace, Chris Sale, was lined up to start Game 3 at home.

Sale didn't have his best stuff, though, allowing seven hits and three earned runs via a pair of home runs, while striking out seven over five innings.

He was ultimately out-dueled by Yamamoto, which is something that has become commonplace for any pitcher that has faced him during playoff baseball over the past couple of seasons.

articles.title: Padres' Michael King Reveals When He Found Out He'd Replace Mason Miller As Closer in Video
articles.summary: After making his first relief appearance of the season to close out the San Diego Padres' 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the NLDS, Michael King revealed when the decision to use him out of the bullpen came about.
articles.body:
After making his first relief appearance of the season to close out the San Diego Padres' 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the NLDS, Michael King revealed when the decision to use him out of the bullpen came about.

Speaking to Fox Sports' Tom Verducci following the game, King said he told Padres manager Craig Stammen after his Game 2 start on Sunday he would be available.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

King, who threw 72 pitches over five innings on Sunday, pitched the final two innings in Game 3 to close out the victory.

The Padres found themselves in need of relief help hours before Game 3 started when All-Star closer Mason Miller was placed on the paternity list when his wife went into labor on Tuesday afternoon.

Padres pitching coach Ruben Niebla said they are "anticipating" Miller will be back for Game 4.

King wasn't necessarily expected to close the game, but availability concerns to other relievers forced the situation.

Stammen told reporters Adrian Morejón, who had 107 strikeouts in 86 innings during the regular season, had "a little stickiness in the shoulder" following his bullpen session on Monday.

Nick Pivetta allowed two runs over 4.1 innings his first appearance of the playoffs. Jason Adam, Yuki Matsui and Bradgley Rodriguez got the Padres through the next 2.2 innings with a one-run lead.

The last time King pitched in relief was Game 3 of the NL Wild Card series against the Chicago Cubs last year.

Milwaukee did threaten in the top of the ninth with back-to-back one-out walks from William Contreras and Ethan Salas, but King got Christian Yelich to ground into a double play to seal the win.

It's the first time King has recorded a save in a game since July 8, 2023, when he was still a member of the New York Yankees.

The Padres won to keep their season alive with Game 4 at Petco Park scheduled for Wednesday at 10 p.m. ET. If San Diego wins again, the series will shift back to Milwaukee for the winner-take-all Game 5 on Friday.

articles.title: Alex Cora reportedly turns down Phillies job again, plans to take off 2027 season
articles.summary: Alex Cora won't manage the Phillies in 2027 after all.
articles.body:
For the second time this year, Alex Cora said no to the Philadelphia Phillies. The former Boston Red Sox manager was reportedly approached by the Phillies for the team's vacant manager role, but once again turned the team down , per multiple reports.

Cora was first approached by the Phillies in April, when the team surprisingly fired Rob Thomson after a slow start . Just days earlier, Cora was fired by the Red Sox, instantly making him the top managerial option on the market.

The Phillies reportedly spoke to Cora at that point about the role, but he decided to take the summer off to be with his family. The Phillies thought Cora might be willing to step back in the dugout after spending much of 2026 at home, but the manager reportedly once again declined the Phillies' job, telling the team he planned to take 2027 off.

Cora's snub leaves the Phillies in a complicated position for next season. With the collective-bargaining agreement ending in December, there's expected to be an owner-imposed lockout during the offseason. During a lockout, team personnel are prohibited from speaking to players, which would complicate matters if the Phillies hired a new, unfamiliar manager.

Because of that, the team could opt to retain interim manager Don Mattingly for another year, per The Athletic. Mattingly took over for Thomson in April and helped lead the Phillies to a postseason berth. He went 79-55 with the club, but couldn't manage the team beyond the wild-card series vs. the Atlanta Braves.

While it was a successful run — especially considering the Phillies' 9-19 start — Mattingly received criticism down the stretch, as the Phillies nearly blew a shot at the playoffs in late September. The manager's in-game tactics faced increased scrutiny during the team's slide, with his bullpen usage, in particular, coming into question.

Prior to managing the Phillies, Mattingly led both the Los Angeles Dodgers and Miami Marlins. His time in Los Angeles was filled with regular-season success, though postseaon glory eluded him. Mattingly made the playoffs just once with the Marlins.

As for Cora, the veteran manager presumably remains the top option on the market. While he was a natural fit with the Phillies given the team's place in the contention cycle and his relationship with general manager Dave Dombrowski (who worked with Cora with the Red Sox), Cora still turned the job down.

That won't stop other teams from getting in touch with Cora, though. And while the manager is signaling he plans to take next season off, that could change if teams start to get more desperate for his services.

articles.title: Blink-182 star gets emotional singing his own song with Padres fans
articles.summary: Blink-182 frontman Tom DeLonge led San Diego Padres fans in an emotional stadium sing-along of 'All the Small Things' in Game 3 against the Brewers.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres have their rally caps on after falling behind 2-0 in their best-of-five MLB playoff series against the Milwaukee Brewers . Thanks to a 4-3 Game 3 win, the Padres now head into Game 4 on Wednesday night with a chance to send the series back to Milwaukee for a win-or-go-home Game 5. But before we dive into tonight's game, there was one unique moment from Game 3 worth watching (at least once) that made for must-see TV thanks to Blink-182 frontman Tom DeLonge.

Blink-182's hit song "All the Small Things" has become an unofficial anthem and late-game tradition for the Padres at Petco Park. But what makes it even more awesome is that DeLonge is a lifelong Padres fan, and during Game 3 of the NLDS matchup with the Brewers, DeLonge was front and center for the sing-along.

Not surprisingly, being in attendance as 40,000-plus fans sing a song you helped create and have performed countless times must have been surreal, and DeLonge was emotional in the moment.

If that's not the perfect sports-and-entertainment crossover moment, I'm not sure what could top it. A team you've loved and a fanbase you've been a part of for your entire life, singing one of your own band's greatest hits in unison during the biggest game of the series? All while the Padres held a 4-3 lead in the bottom of the 8th inning? This is the kind of sports moment you typically can only find in movies.

DeLonge has spoken about his love for the Padres in various interviews over the years, including one in 2016 with MLB.com . So there's no question DeLonge's love for the franchise left him going through the same whirlwind of emotions that all Padres fans had on Tuesday night.

Also, kudos to DeLonge for not letting the emotional moment overwhelm him beyond a sing-along that was obviously tugging on his heartstrings. I can say with certainty that if he and I changed spots, the water works would have been flowing.

articles.title: New MLB Rumors on Don Mattingly, Phillies' Managerial Search After Alex Cora Snub
articles.summary: After serving as the Philadelphia Phillies' interim manager for most of the 2026 season, naming Don Mattingly the full-time manager for 2027 is reportedly under consideration.
articles.body:
After serving as the Philadelphia Phillies' interim manager for most of the 2026 season, naming Don Mattingly the full-time manager for 2027 is reportedly under consideration.

According to Matt Gelb and Jayson Stark of The Athletic, "everything remains on the table" for the Phillies in their managerial search, including removing the interim tag from Mattingly.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

One huge domino has already fallen and improved Mattingly's chances of landing the job, as Bob Nightengale of USA Today reported this week that former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora declined to speak with the Phillies about their vacancy, noting that he plans on taking 2027 off.

Per Gelb and Stark, Mattingly is still under contract through 2027 as the Phillies' bench coach, and he is expected to remain with the organization regardless of whether he is named the manager.

If the Phillies go in a different managerial direction, Mattingly reportedly could serve as a front-office advisor under his son, Preston Mattingly, who is the Phillies' general manager.

The elder Mattingly has to be considered a strong candidate for several reasons, including the job he did in Philadelphia this season.

Mattingly replaced Rob Thomson as the Phillies' manager 28 games into the campaign with the team sitting at 9-19.

From that point forward, Mattingly led the Phillies to a 79-55 mark and got them to the playoffs for the fifth consecutive season.

The Phillies fell to the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card Series, but they took the Braves to a decisive third game and put up a strong fight throughout the series.

One thing that could potentially work against Mattingly is the controversial decision he made with his bullpen in Game 1.

With a 3-2 lead, Mattingly surprisingly turned to closer Jhoan Durán in the seventh inning rather than waiting until the ninth.

Durán proceeded to allow two hits and three earned runs over two innings, blowing the save and losing the game.

While that decision may be second-guessed for quite some time, Mattingly does bring a wealth of experience and a solid amount of managerial success to the table.

Over his 13 seasons as manager of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Miami Marlins and Phillies, Mattingly has posted a 968-1,005 record and reached the playoffs five times.

The longtime New York Yankees first baseman was also named National League Manager of the Year in 2020 when he took the Marlins to the playoffs with a 31-29 record during the COVID-shortened season.

While the Phillies manager job figures to be a desirable one due to the presence of star players such as Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo, the organization could be hard-pressed to find a more qualified option than Mattingly.

articles.title: Freddie Freeman on his approach to hitting Chris Sale: 'You've got to be prepared to die'
articles.summary: Freddie Freeman has tagged Chris Sale for multiple home runs over their careers.
articles.body:
Over his career, Atlanta Braves starter Chris Sale has been extremely effective against lefties. His arm slot, combined with his nasty stuff, make Sale a nightmare matchup for same-handed hitters, who have slugged just .285 against Sale over his career.

But Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman isn't most hitters. Freeman — who, like Sale, is heading to the Hall of Fame one day — has excelled where most lefties have failed. In 16 regular-season at-bats, Freeman has hit .313 against Sale, with two home runs.

That success reared its head Tuesday night, when Freeman tagged Sale for a solo home run in the fourth inning of the Dodgers' 3-1 win over the Braves in the NLDS.

After the contest, Freeman gave a pretty serious answer when asked about his approach to facing Sale, telling Fox, "You've got to be prepared to die" in the batter's box.

While that sounds … a bit extreme … there was a lot of logic behind Freeman's full quote, which read:

"Anything against Chris, you're trying to find something positive going in … he's one of the best pitchers in this game. You're just really trying to hope he makes a mistake and you're on time for it, really. "It's an extremely hard at-bat for a lefty. Like, I always say against him, 'You've got to be prepared to die.' Really, that's the mindset. If you pull off of him, you've got no chance. He's throwing behind you, so if he hits you in the ear, you've gotta be OK with it. That's kinda my mentality."

"Anything against Chris, you're trying to find something positive going in … he's one of the best pitchers in this game. You're just really trying to hope he makes a mistake and you're on time for it, really.

"It's an extremely hard at-bat for a lefty. Like, I always say against him, 'You've got to be prepared to die.' Really, that's the mindset. If you pull off of him, you've got no chance. He's throwing behind you, so if he hits you in the ear, you've gotta be OK with it. That's kinda my mentality."

Freeman's comment drew laughs from the Fox crew, including former Boston Red Sox designated hitter David Ortiz, who also hit Sale well during his career.

While Freeman's comment about mortality will get the most attention, what he said directly after that is more important. Given Sale's arm slot, lefties have to be committed to staying in the batter's box at all times. The instant they bail out, thinking they are about to be hit with a pitch, they put themselves at a massive disadvantage against Sale's stuff.

Because of that, Freeman goes into each at-bat against Sale determined to stay in the box no matter what. If that means he gets hit by a pitch, Freeman is OK with that. It's a better result than striking out, something many, many lefties have done against Sale over his career.

articles.title: Juan Soto’s record-setting $765 million contract could reshape the New York Mets star’s long-term fortune through salary, investments, taxes and future financial leverage
articles.summary: Juan Soto's landmark $765 million contract with the New York Mets not only sets a record in MLB history but also offers significant implications for his financial strategy, including investments, taxes, and long-term wealth accumulation. Discover how this contract changes the landscape of baseball earnings and Soto's economic leverage.
articles.body: Juan Soto’s move to the New York Mets created one of the biggest financial stories in baseball history. The 15-year, $765 million agreement, finalized in December 2024, remains MLB’s largest contract by total value and carries a $51 million average annual value. The deal also includes a $75 million signing bonus and no deferred money, giving the star a particularly direct path from baseball earnings to long-term wealth.According to Celebrity Net Worth, Juan Soto’s net worth is estimated at $100 million, although such estimates can change as salary, endorsements, investments and taxes evolve. His Mets agreement could significantly alter that figure over the next decade and beyond, particularly because the contract provides substantial guaranteed earnings while retaining an important future decision point.Juan Soto’s $765 million Mets contract reshapes MLB’s financial landscapeSoto’s contract fundamentally changes the scale of baseball earnings. The agreement covers 15 seasons through 2039 and guarantees $765 million, while the $75 million signing bonus provides an additional early source of liquidity within the overall deal, and the contract also contains a full no-trade clause, reinforcing Soto’s control over where he plays during the agreement.The absence of deferred money is particularly significant. Unlike contracts that push substantial compensation into future decades, Soto’s agreement does not rely on delaying hundreds of millions of dollars. That means the economic value of his compensation is not reduced by a long wait for payment, although taxes, investment performance and inflation will still influence the eventual value of his wealth.Soto can therefore potentially deploy substantial earnings during his prime playing years. Real estate, financial markets, private businesses and other investments could provide avenues for diversification, although specific private investments should not be assumed without public documentation.Shohei Ohtani’s deferrals create stark contrastThe structure becomes clearer when compared with Shohei Ohtani’s $700 million Los Angeles Dodgers contract. Ohtani agreed to defer $680 million, receiving $2 million annually during the 10-year playing term before the deferred payments begin in 2034 and continue through 2043.That arrangement created a dramatic contrast with Soto’s immediate-payment structure. MLB’s reporting noted that Ohtani’s contract had a much lower present value because of those deferrals, while Soto’s deal contains no such mechanism.For Soto, the financial advantage is flexibility. Money earned earlier can potentially be invested earlier, allowing compound growth to become a larger component of his long-term fortune.Juan Soto’s opt-out adds future leverageDespite signing for 15 seasons, Soto does not necessarily have to remain tied to the contract for its entire original duration. His agreement includes an opt-out after the 2029 season, when he would be 31.The Mets can prevent that opt-out by increasing the average annual value of the final 10 seasons from $51 million to $55 million. If that happens, the total value of the contract would rise from $765 million to $805 million.That clause gives Soto significant future leverage. articles.title: X expands its 'Gametime' sports hub beyond the NFL, starting with MLB | TechCrunch
articles.summary: X is turning its NFL-focused Gametime feature into a year-round sports destination, starting with MLB and with other professional leagues to follow.
articles.body:
X is doubling down on sports, with Wednesday’s news that it’s expanding its “Gametime” feature on the social media site to go beyond tracking the NFL alone.

First announced in August, NFL Gametime is X’s new project that offers a single hub for tracking live scores, getting play-by-play updates, tuning into game feeds, and more. The move wasn’t meant to be useful only to X users who like to congregate on the platform to discuss live sporting events, but to woo brands and advertisers looking to reach passionate sports fans.

At Advertising Week New York, X said Gametime will become a year-round destination spanning “all professional sports.”

However, that full expansion isn’t yet live as of today. Instead, X announced its second league partnership with Major League Baseball (MLB). Arriving this month, the new MLB experience will allow baseball fans to follow and engage in postseason discussions and will organize things like scores and stats, team and league content, plus news, creator content, and real-time discussions.

X said content from other leagues will be added soon, including the NBA.

The expansion of the Gametime feature comes as X continues its efforts to win back advertisers — in this case by leveraging live sports and their highly engaged fans as a way to draw brands back to X.

“In just six weeks, Gametime has evolved from a football-focused product into a scalable destination for sports, attracting strong demand across major advertisers from payments to consumer goods looking to engage highly attentive fans from the pregame conversation through the biggest moments of the game,” said SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, Monique Pintarelli, in an announcement.

The new feature’s introduction follows X owner Elon Musk’s July settlement in a multiyear legal battle with the advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), which X had sued for its alleged “illegal boycott” of the platform.

Some advertisers had become uncomfortable with the platform’s lax moderation standards under Musk, as well as with Musk’s outsized position on the social media site, where he often spouted controversial views and politics via X posts. Musk believed the WFA’s guidelines had steered brands and ad agencies away from X, suggesting it was a place where their ads could appear next to harmful online content.

X’s announcement of the settlement in July said the move “resets the relationship between the two organizations.” The company also committed to both freedom of speech and brand-safety innovations.
