articles.title: Padres activate closer Mason Miller from paternity list ahead of must-win Game 4 vs. Brewers
articles.summary: Miller missed Game 3 on Tuesday for the birth of his first child.
articles.body:
The San Diego Padres have their closer back.

One day after the team added reliever Mason Miller to the postseason paternity list, he has been activated and is available to pitch in Game 4 on Wednesday.

Miller missed San Diego's must-win Game 3 on Tuesday, with the Padres down 2-0 in the best-of-five series. San Diego rallied for a 4-3 win . The Padres still trail 2-1 in the series and must win Wednesday to force a Friday night series finale.

The closer was replaced on the roster with Wandy Peralta. Peralta did not appear Tuesday and has now been removed from the roster as Miller returns.

Miller and his wife, Jordan, welcomed their first child, and everything went well, per manager Craig Stammen .

In Game 3, San Diego took a one-run lead in the top of the eighth. While Miller would normally have gotten the call out of the pen to get six big outs, in his absence, Stammen turned to starter Michael King.

The veteran right-hander began his career as a reliever and later became a starter. King allowed just one hit and walked two in his appearance, but he gave up no runs and struck out one batter. Stammen said King would be available for Game 4 if needed.

With their season on the line, the Padres are starting Walker Buehler. The 32-year-old has pitched in 32 games this season and has a 9-6 record with a 4.63 ERA.

Stammen will likely turn to the pen at the first sign of trouble, especially because the manager said the team hopes to have setup man Adrian Morejon available tonight as well.

articles.title: Guardians Beat White Sox to Stay Alive, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The Cleveland Guardians kept their season alive with a 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, forcing a decisive Game 4.
articles.body:
The Cleveland Guardians kept their season alive with a 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, forcing a decisive Game 4.

With a chance to seal the series win, No. 6 Chicago entered the matchup as 1.5-point favorites over Cleveland on Wednesday, per FanDuel Sportsbook , but crumbled under pressure at Rate Field in Chicago.

With their backs against the wall, the No. 2 Guardians turned to Jo Adell and Jose Ramirez, who combined for five RBIs after Cleveland dropped the first two games of the series at home.

The pitching staff also more than did their part with a historic performance:

No. 6 Chicago White Sox def. No. 3 Houston Astros, 2-0

No. 4 New York Yankees def. No. 5 Boston Red Sox, 2-0

No. 3 Atlanta Braves def. No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies, 2-1

No. 4 San Diego Padres def. No. 5 Chicago Cubs, 2-0

No. 6 Chicago White Sox lead No. 2 Cleveland Guardians, 2-1

No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays lead No. 4 New York Yankees, 2-0

No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers lead No. 3 Atlanta Braves, 2-1

No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers lead No. 4 San Diego Padres, 2-1

Despite a strong start for the White Sox, forcing the Guardians to go down in order in the top of the first and scoring a quick run on a Kyle Teel RBI in the bottom, the game did a 180 in the top of the third with a four-run inning for the Guardians.

Steven Kwan brought in Travis Bazzana to tie it 1-1, prompting a pitching change for the Sox. Jo Adell tripled deep to right, bringing in three RBIs and giving the Guardians a 4-1 lead heading into the bottom of the third.

Chicago's Tristan Peters attempted to chip away at the Guardians' lead with a double that scored Chase Meidroth, cutting the deficit to 4-2 after four innings

Chase DeLauter answered for the Guardians, driving in Jose Ramirez with an RBI in the next inning. Ramirez scored with an impressive slide into home, restoring Cleveland's three-run lead.

The Guardians turned offense into defense in the bottom of the fifth, turning a double play with two runners in scoring position to escape the inning.

The bases were loaded with two outs when Chicago's Sam Antonacci stepped to the plate. The designated hitter was hit by a pitch, forcing in Braden Montgomery and cutting the Guardians' lead to 5-3.

Miguel Vargas faced a full count with the bases loaded before grounding out to Ramirez, allowing the Guardians to escape what could have been a disastrous inning while giving up just one run.

Cleveland added two runs in the top of the eighth on a Ramirez triple that drove in Bazzana and Patrick Bailey to take a 7-3 lead.

The Guardians showed they were not ready to end their season yet, adding two insurance runs in the top of the ninth as Angel Genao and Brayan Rocchio got in on the offensive action with an RBI each, forcing the White Sox to face three more outs with a six-run deficit.

The White Sox were unable to overcome the deficit, going down in order in the bottom of the ninth.

Surviving elimination, the Guardians and White Sox will remain in Chicago for Game 4, as the White Sox get another chance to put Cleveland away. First pitch is scheduled for Thursday at 5 p.m. ET.

They scored eight runs in four games and never could find the big hit they needed to build a big inning against Yamamoto or Glasnow. articles.title: MLB Playoff Divisional Round Overreactions to Dodgers vs. Braves, Rays vs. Yankees and Every Game
articles.summary: When the summer doldrums start to wear you down as a baseball fan, dreaming about days like these can quickly put that pep back in your step.
articles.body:
When the summer doldrums start to wear you down as a baseball fan, dreaming about days like these can quickly put that pep back in your step.

Four postseason games, back-to-back-to-back-to-back.

All of them are potential elimination games, no less.

And we've celebrated the occasion with one rapid (over)reaction for each of the eight teams in action.

Cleveland Guardians: They Done Woke Up J-Ram

For most of this season, José Ramírez simply wasn't the J-Ram we've come to know and love.

Even before suffering that broken hamate in mid-June, he was only on pace for 22 home runs and 74 RBI, both of which would have been his worst (non-2020) totals since 2016.

But he really was not the same after his return to the lineup.

In his last 52 regular-season games, Ramírez hit just two home runs and posted a .593 OPS.

And in the first two postseason games against the White Sox, he went 0-for-6 with two walks and three strikeouts.

At long last, though, the proverbial light may have come back on.

J-Ram went 2-for-4 with a double, a triple, a stolen base and a walk in Wednesday's 9-3 win over Chicago.

Even his unsuccessful plate appearances were impressive. The lineout in the first inning was scalded at 107.9 MPH with an expected batting average of .830. It just happened to find Randal Grichuk's glove. He also worked the count full before popping out in the seventh inning.

But it was the double-stolen base-run scored on a grounder sequence in the fifth inning that felt like the J-Ram of yore. And the two-run triple in the eighth made it feel like more than a flash in the pan.

If he's back—with Parker Messick pitching Thursday and Gavin Williams gearing up for Game 5—Cleveland might storm back from a 2-0 deficit.

(Also, three cheers to Foster Griffin, who struck out seven of the 11 batters he faced to get the win. He had a 5.19 ERA after relocating from Washington at the trade deadline, but that was huge.)

Chicago White Sox: The Bullpen Shtick Has Finally Imploded

In winning their first four postseason games, the Chicago White Sox's MVP was the entire bullpen.

Of the total 36 innings pitched in those victories, the bullpen was responsible for 26.0, doing so with a 1.04 ERA, 0.69 WHIP and 10.4 K/9.

It was as if they all of a sudden had nine Josh Haders out there. (Houston's Hader finished the year with a 1.01 ERA, 0.76 WHIP and 11.1 K/9 in his 44.2 innings of dominance.)

But after Sean Newcomb gave them two scoreless innings in starting Game 3, the wheels came all the way off.

Starting with Bryan Hudson, the subsequent six White Sox pitchers took turns getting smoked to the tune of 10 hits, 10 walks and nine earned runs as the Guardians lived to see another day.

Notably, Jordan Hicks and Grant Taylor played no part in that implosion. The former has gone 10.1 scoreless innings with 18 strikeouts since Labor Day, while the latter has been quietly one of MLB's most dominant relievers since July 4.

All the same, the dam may have broken on Wednesday.

A very limited supply of reliable pitching was everyone's concern about the White Sox heading into the postseason, and it finally reared its ugly head in Game 3.

Can they reel it back in on Thursday, presumably with Erick Fedde and Taylor each pitching multiple innings?

Los Angeles Dodgers: There Is No Achilles' Heel

Less than one month ago, the thought of Edwin Díaz pitching in anything close to a high-leverage situation for the Dodgers was inconceivable.

In 16 appearances across two trips to the IL, he posted a 11.85 ERA and blew four of his last seven save chances.

But something clicked during his last rehab assignment.

Over his final five regular-season appearances, he struck out nine of 17 batters faced while allowing just two baserunners. And after pitching a flawless sixth inning in Game 2, Dave Roberts had seen enough to put him back in the closer role for Games 3 and 4.

He locked them both down, not even allowing a baserunner in the series clincher.

Meanwhile, the hero in both Games 3 and 4 came out of the 9-hole in the lineup.

After not even getting a plate appearance in Game 1 or Game 2, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning in Game 3 to break a scoreless tie, ultimately driving in the winning run.

On Wednesday night, Andy Pages delivered a massive two-out, two-run single that put the Dodgers ahead for good.

Of course, with this loaded roster, the 9-hole has never been much of a hole.

During the regular season, they had an MLB-best .259 batting average from that bottom spot in the order. But those two games in Atlanta were a sobering reminder that there are no easy outs when facing the twice-reigning champs.

Atlanta Braves: It Might Be Time to Trade Ronald Acuña Jr.

Ronald Acuña Jr. is a five-time All-Star and a three-time Silver Slugger.

He was the NL Rookie of the Year in 2018 and the NL MVP in 2023.

When he's at his best, not many who have ever played the game have been better.

But he sure has been a ghost in October for a while now.

Dating back to Game 2 of the 2020 NLDS against Miami, Acuña has gone 14-for-84 (.167 AVG) with 24 strikeouts, zero home runs and just one RBI in 24 games played.

The idea of Atlanta trading away its final two years of team control on Acuña would have been considered blasphemy just a few days ago. Braves fans certainly sang his praises when he played a massive role in keeping the Phillies at bay in the first half of September.

But here at the end of his third consecutive injury-plagued season, the fans sure seem to have had enough of his inability to deliver when they need him the most, going 0-for-6 with runners in scoring position this postseason.

We'll leave the "Where would he go?" and "How much could they get?" speculations for another day, but it does feel like the Braves need to do something drastic to shake things up after yet another early flameout in October.

Tampa Bay Rays: Welcome to the Victor Mesa Jr. Show

For most of the regular season, I was reluctant to believe the Tampa Bay Rays could win the World Series.

It's not because of their payroll, nor the fact that they have never won it all before.

Rather, it's because, for most of the season, it felt like they could get swept in a series if Junior Caminero and/or Yandy Díaz went through a cold spell. So much of this offense depended on that dynamic duo in the first half of the year.

Chandler Simpson really started to heat up in July, though. They traded for Liam Hicks in August, bolstering a problematic catcher spot in the lineup. But the final, biggest nudge that pushed the Rays into Serious Contender-ville came when Victor Mesa Jr. caught fire in September.

The rookie had a 1.015 OPS in the final month of the regular season, blossoming into a near-daily fixture in the lineup.

And after catching that controversial Spencer Jones fly ball off the catwalk early in Game 2 in Tampa Bay, Mesa delivered the 401-foot haymaker of a two-run home run off Max Fried in the sixth inning.

Fried had allowed just four home runs during the regular season.

His 0.32 HR/9 rate was the lowest among pitchers in a season with at least 100 innings pitched since 2014.

He hadn't allowed a single home run to a left-handed hitter all season.

That's how legends are born, though. And Mesa's postseason legend might just be getting started.

Aaron Boone isn't to blame for Aaron Judge's postseason absence.

It's not Aaron Boone's fault that the Yankees couldn't field their way out of a paper bag in Game 2 of this series against the Rays.

It's not Aaron Boone's fault that Ryan Vilade's deep fly ball traveled just beyond Spencer Jones' outstretched glove, nor that Anthony Volpe's deep fly ball a few innings later traveled only far enough for a fan-interference decision heard 'round the world.

It's not Aaron Boone's fault that Max Fried picked the worst possible moment to allow his first home run to a left-handed hitter (Victor Mesa Jr.) since August 2025, more than 30 starts ago.

And we know this because nothing ever seems to be Aaron Boone's fault.

How can the Yankees justify keeping him once again after yet another embarrassing postseason exit?

He is now 27-30 in the postseason in his nine-year managerial career, and has overseen more than 50 percent of what is now a 17-year drought without a World Series title.

On the one hand, many MLB fan bases would do anything to experience 57 postseason games in less than a decade.

On the other hand, six-ish postseason games per year is pretty much the bare minimum when you're the Damn Yankees.

George Steinbrenner would've fired Boone at least four times by now. And if Hal Steinbrenner doesn't do it now, he might as well put out a public statement that simply making the playoffs (while turning a profit) is the new Yankee Way.

Milwaukee Brewers: We'll Be Talking About "The Garrett Mitchell Game" for Years

For years, Milwaukee Brewers fans had been wondering what Garrett Mitchell could do at full strength.

After going 20th overall in the 2020 draft, his "games played" count through his first half-decade in the pros was 64, 96, 27, 83 and 29, suffering one injury after another.

At long last, though, he had a healthy season in 2026, becoming Milwaukee's primary center fielder behind the strength of his blistering speed.

And in the series-clinching victory over the Padres, he was everywhere.

It was Mitchell's single up the middle in the third inning that produced the first run of the night.

It was Mitchell's leadoff triple in the fifth inning that set the table for Jackson Chourio's game-winning RBI.

And it was Mitchell's home run robbery of Manny Machado in the eighth inning that saved the game while evoking memories of Adam Jones' catch in the 2017 World Baseball Classic.

Previously, "The Garrett Mitchell Game" was Game 2 in the 2024 wild card round against the Mets, when his two-run home run broke an eighth inning tie and brought the Brewers a season-saving victory.

That was one moment, though, and quickly forgotten when they collapsed the following night.

This was his game, setting up the NLCS rematch with the Dodgers.

Does he have a few more tricks up his sleeve?

San Diego Padres: Never Going to Get Over the Hump

The San Diego Padres entered the NLDS hotter than a thousand suns.

They won 17 of their final 20 regular season games, leading the majors in runs scored during that time.

They also breezed through the wild card round against the Cubs, shutting down the best offense in baseball by a combined score of 12-1.

But as they always eventually do, they ran out of gas in painstaking fashion.

With help from the roof at American Family Field, they blew an early 2-0 lead in losing Game 1.

In Game 2, the greatest closer in all the land may or may not have been tipping his pitches for another heartbreaking loss.

And after clawing back to take Game 3, Manny Machado's would-be game-tying home run in Game 4 wasn't meant to be, as this scorching hot offense was extinguished in a 3-1 loss.

It's becoming an all-too-familiar tale in San Diego.

They scored just one run in each of their losses in last year's wild card round.

They blew a 2-1 series lead in the 2024 NLDS by failing to score for 24 consecutive innings.

And let's not even talk about Josh Hader's availability with two innings remaining in the 2022 NLCS.

Despite Machado, Fernando Tatis Jr., Xander Bogaerts and more, it's just never enough for a team that is starting to feel destined to never win a World Series.

For now, they're tied with the Brewers as the longest-existing franchises to have never won it all.

We'll see in a few weeks' time whether that's still the case.

articles.title: MLB Lays Out Lockout Plans in New Rumors, Includes No Contact with Players, Names Removed from Sites
articles.summary: The MLB playoffs have taken center stage in October, but there is still a potential lockout looming.
articles.body:
The MLB playoffs have taken center stage in October, but there is still a potential lockout looming.

And the league is reportedly taking steps to prepare.

Evan Drellich of The Athletic reported Wednesday that Dan Halem, who is second-in-command to commissioner Rob Manfred, shared a confidential, 34-page memo with team owners and high-ranking executives that detailed what should happen if there is a lockout.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Some parts are intuitive, such as the call for no business between MLB players on 40-man rosters and teams while there is a work stoppage. That means there will be no new trades or signings like there would be during a normal offseason.

What's more, team officials must try to avoid player interactions "to the greatest extent possible," per Harlem.

They can still be "cordial" should they run into a player in public, but they cannot talk business even if they attend a player's wedding. The guidance even goes as far as to tell teams to avoid sending holiday cards to players during a work stoppage.

Notably, the league will not stop players from playing in other professional leagues in Japan or elsewhere, although Harlem stressed the focus is on avoiding a lockout entirely.

"Our commitment has been and remains to exhaust every realistic option to achieve our goal of reaching an agreement with the Players Association," he wrote. "However, clubs need to be prepared for the possibility that an agreement will not be reached by then and the clubs are left with no realistic alternative but to implement a lockout of major league players."

Fans missing baseball won't even be able to turn to official team and league websites if there is a lockout, as player images and videos must be "scrubbed" just like they were during the 2021-22 lockout.

However, teams can still sell merchandise with the players' names and images since the right to do so comes from outside business arrangements rather than the collective bargaining agreement.

There will inevitably be some communication between teams and agents since the latter represent minor league players as well, but the memo stressed that "the scope of any agent communications must be monitored and strictly controlled" so there are no discussions regarding players on the 40-man roster.

For now, the focus remains on coming to terms on a new collective bargaining agreement.

But the preparations have already started for a lockout, and they are quite detailed.

articles.title: Yankees 2026 Offseason Guide on Free Agents, Trade Targets, More Roster Shakeups After ALDS Loss
articles.summary: Well, it's official: The New York Yankees are mired in their longest World Series drought in more than a century.
articles.body:
Well, it's official: The New York Yankees are mired in their longest World Series drought in more than a century.

With Wednesday's loss to the Tampa Bay Rays, we are now guaranteed a 17th consecutive world champion that isn't the Bronx Bombers, breaking the previous past-century record of 16 in a row from 1979-1995. (Excluding 1994, when there was no World Series.)

As has been the case on an annual basis in recent years, the immediate question is whether the Yankees will stick with Aaron Boone as manager or shake things up. He has one year left on the extension they gave him two Februaries ago, but the seat is hotter than ever.

Once that part is settled, though, it'll be on to the roster moves meant to end this embarrassing drought.

Ahead, we'll take a look at New York's most noteworthy free agents and its best options for replacing them—whether internally, via free agency or via trade—before offering up a super early look at what the Yankees' 26-man roster might look like on Opening Day.

Many Yankees fans turned a cold shoulder to Chisholm as he fell well short of his preseason promise of a 50/50 season . (That fielding blunder in Game 2 against Tampa Bay didn't help matters.)

However, they'll likely extend him the estimated one-year, $23.1M qualifying offer. After all, he reached 19 home runs and 41 stolen bases, bringing his "since the beginning of 2021" totals to 125 and 169, respectively. Those numbers match Bobby Witt Jr. (123 and 193) and Trea Turner (130 and 165), even though Chisholm has received 539 fewer plate appearances than the former and 1,108 fewer than the latter.

He'll likely reject the offer, though, and seek something closer to the nine-figure payday most analysts anticipated heading into this season. And with George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe and José Caballero all available for middle infield duties for the foreseeable future, New York likely won't be the one giving him that mega deal.

Beyond Chisholm, both Grisham and Goldschmidt are considerable losses, each playing in more than 100 games this season.

They aren't exactly deal-breaker losses, though. Spencer Jones is arguably already better than Grisham and should be the everyday center fielder in 2027. And though they'll miss Goldy's bat against left-handed pitching, having a right-handed platoon bat for Ben Rice is no longer the necessity it seemed to be one year ago.

All six of these pitchers are relievers.

That is wonderful news for New York's fully intact, arguably too-crowded starting rotation, but problematic for the bullpen, to say the least.

Bednar is the biggest one by far, owner of 35 saves and a 2.47 ERA this season. Like Chisholm, he could also be headed for a qualifying offer of an estimated $23.1M, but is expected to decline it in pursuit of something closer to a four-year, $66M contract.

If he does walk, there's no obvious in-house option to take his place. The only returning Yankee who recorded any saves for them in 2026 is Fernando Cruz—and he's trying to rehab a partially torn UCL without surgery.

Also, if they do let Bednar walk, it would be the first time they've needed to replace a pitcher with at least 35 saves since Andrew Miller took David Robertson's place during the 2014-15 offseason.

Notably, Blackburn was worth even more wins above replacement than Bednar, per Baseball-Reference . In fact, B-R graded Blackburn as the third-most valuable reliever in all of baseball, tied with Mason Miller and trailing only Jhoan Duran and Louis Varland. (That sure did come out of nowhere, though, as Blackburn entered 2026 with a 5.22 ERA over the previous eight seasons.)

As we just discussed, not only is David Bednar headed for free agency, but so are Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill and Ryan Yarbrough.

That's four of the five Yankees pitchers who logged at least 55 relief innings in 2026, leaving Brent Headrick as one of the few established bullpen guys still under contract.

Not only is this New York's biggest need, but it might also be just about their entire offseason focus.

Austin Wells at least turned things around at the dish for a respectable finish after entering the All-Star Break with a horrendous .504 OPS. And behind the plate, he won the third-most ABS challenges among catchers in 2026.

Still, Yankees catchers had some of the worst offensive numbers in the majors, batting .196 as a group. It's still hard to believe they did nothing to address that ahead of the trade deadline, since it was even worse then.

Even with Jazz Chisholm Jr. likely out of the picture, this is more of a "luxury want" than a "desperate need."

If the Yankees simply do nothing and go into 2027 with Ryan McMahon at third base, George Lombard Jr. at shortstop, Anthony Volpe at second base, Ben Rice at first base, José Caballero as the 3B/SS backup and Luis García Jr. as the 1B/2B backup, it certainly wouldn't be the worst infield situation on Opening Day.

But the Yankees can make "luxury want" signings, and guys like Brandon Lowe and Luis Arraez are there for the taking.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Now that George Lombard Jr. is no longer a prospect, New York's top player in the farm system is probably shortstop Dax Kilby . Don't expect to see him any time soon, though. The now 19-year-old was their first-round draft pick in 2025, but he missed most of this season with a hamstring injury. He hasn't even progressed to High-A Hudson Valley, let alone Double-A or Triple-A.

The two most likely to factor into the mix in 2027 are right-handed pitchers Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange .

The former made six big-league starts this season, including a quality start against Houston in late August. (He was also scheduled to start the season finale before it got rained out.) However, he kept getting sent back down to Triple-A once the high-priced starter he was filling in for was able to return from injury, and could be in a similar "break in case of emergency" role next year.

The latter was a starter for the first couple of months at Triple-A before transitioning into a relief role. Had he not missed about 10 weeks with a shoulder injury, he likely would have been in the big-league bullpen in 2026. Got to like his chances of making the cut for next year's 'pen, given all that they're losing from that position group.

Pete Fairbanks is also available. Maybe Kenley Jansen and Carlos Estévez, too, if their club options are declined. But Bednar and Iglesias are the clear top options for any team looking to sign an established closer.

The deciding factor between the two options is how committed the Yankees are willing to be.

Bednar is heading into his age-32 season and should be able to command at least a three-year deal, if not four years. Iglesias, on the other hand, turns 37 in January and might be gettable on a one-year deal. (Either one is likely to sign for an AAV in the $15M-$17M range.)

Closers get all of the bullpen love, but very few relief pitchers have been more consistently dominant over the past three seasons than San Diego's Morejón. He relies heavily on his sinker, but his four-pitch arsenal was solid, leading to more than 100 strikeouts in 2026 alone.

Maybe they even sign him as the closer after he set up admirably for Robert Suarez and Mason Miller for years? He'd also be a great target for eighth-inning duties in Paul Blackburn's stead.

Everyone expected the Yankees to trade for Jeffers, right up until the Twins got hot in late July and decided to be buyers instead of sellers.

Jeffers has had a .782 OPS over the past four seasons, one of the 10 or so most valuable catchers in the sport during that time. Whether he supplants Austin Wells as the primary catcher or it's more of a 50/50 split, he could be a major addition to New York's lineup.

Good luck finding a second baseman who can match both Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s power and speed, but Brandon Lowe would certainly handle the first with 66 home runs and an .806 OPS over the past two seasons. And Yankee Stadium's short porch in right would be conducive to his left-handed power.

Before we get into the actual players New York could target, let's note that the Yankees are in a tremendous position to wheel and deal.

As is, the big four in the starting rotation are Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, each of whom is signed through at least 2028. And for the No. 5 spot in that rotation, it's an absurd logjam of Will Warren, Ryan Weathers, Luis Gil, Clarke Schmidt and Elmer Rodriguez—with Schmidt the only member of that bunch who isn't under team control for at least two more seasons.

It's an embarrassment of riches. And while they could mimic the Dodgers by hoarding those arms like a dragon guarding a treasure pile, they'll probably try to trade at least one of those candidates for the No. 5 spot to upgrade elsewhere.

Remember late July? When the Padres were 50-53, 11th in the NL standings and everyone started speculating about a second straight summer with a Mason Miller blockbuster?

That never happened, obviously, but could Miller (with three years of arbitration eligibility remaining) be the belle of this winter's trade block ball?

We'll say this much for the Padres: They desperately need to address their 2027 starting rotation. Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Walker Buehler are unrestricted free agents. Michael King can opt out of the two years left on his contract and is all but guaranteed to do so.

If he does, the Padres are looking at a mess, hoping Yu Darvish returns at 40 after missing all of 2026 and that Joe Musgrove can amount to something after missing both 2025 and 2026.

Trading Miller for a package of Luis Gil and Will Warren could be their saving grace.

Between Freddy Peralta this past winter, Devin Williams the previous year and Corbin Burnes the offseason before that, we have plenty of evidence that the Brewers are not afraid to trade away a star player ahead of his final season of team control.

Nor should they be afraid, as they inexplicably just keep getting better every time they do it.

Well, William Contreras has a $14.5M club option for 2027. The Brewers could definitely benefit from another starting pitcher or two in a rotation that can get questionable quickly beyond Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson.

While Milwaukee might be actively shopping Contreras, De La Cruz is far more of an "at least make them say no" trade candidate.

But with the never-ending reports of De La Cruz refusing to even engage in long-term extension talks with the Reds, the Yankees should make them say no.

They would at least need to offer up George Lombard Jr., probably Spencer Jones and at least one of the aforementioned "maybe the No. 5 option in 2027" starting pitchers to even raise an eyebrow from Cincinnati's front office. But if they could pull it off, it would give the Yankees at least three years' worth of a superstar at shortstop instead of their current plan of a revolving door in the middle infield.

Starting Lineup (vs. Blue Jays RHP Dylan Cease)

1B Ben Rice RF Aaron Judge LF Cody Bellinger DH Giancarlo Stanton 2B Luis García Jr. C William Contreras CF Spencer Jones 3B Ryan McMahon SS George Lombard Jr.

C Austin Wells IF Anthony Volpe UTIL José Caballero OF Heliot Ramos or Jasson Dominguez

RHP Cam Schlittler LHP Max Fried RHP Gerrit Cole LHP Carlos Rodón RHP Will Warren

RHP David Bednar LHP Adrián Morejón LHP Brent Headrick RHP Kevin Ginkel RHP Yerry De Los Santos RHP Carlos Lagrange RHP Clarke Schmidt RHP Fernando Cruz

Even with Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham and Paul Goldschmidt all expected to walk, the only significant changes we're projecting among the position players are a healthy Giancarlo Stanton at DH, Luis García Jr. shifting from first base back to second base and a trade for William Contreras. If they can't pry him away from Milwaukee, signing Ryan Jeffers is also very much on the table.

For the rotation, Will Warren is the guess for the No. 5 spot, as he has logged more innings over the past two seasons than any other Yankee. Clarke Schmidt sticks around in a bulk relief role in his final season before hitting free agency, while Ryan Weathers and Luis Gil are strong candidates to be traded this winter.

In the bullpen, re-signing David Bednar is the top priority, followed shortly by landing the best reliever available this winter in LHP Adrián Morejón. They still have other work to do, especially if Fernando Cruz can't rehab that partially torn UCL. Kevin Ginkel is a total dart throw, but he is one of many free agents who could enter New York's sixth/seventh inning mix in 2027.

articles.summary: The New York Yankees were back home for Game 3 of their ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night, hoping to avoid a sweep. But Yankee Stadium itself played an instrumental role in what was ultimately a disappointing night for the team.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees were back home for Game 3 of their ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night, hoping to avoid a sweep. But Yankee Stadium itself played an instrumental role in what was ultimately a disappointing night for the team.

Ryan Vilade's homer that barely snuck over the short perch in right field, Victor Mesa Jr.'s moonshot to that same part of the park and an Anthony Volpe blast that was initially ruled a homer before being overturned due to fan interference all played a huge role in Tampa's 4-3 win, ending the series.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Here's a look at the game's top performers:

Here's an updated look at the MLB bracket:

The Rays may have swept the Yankees, but it was hardly a one-sided series, and Wednesday's finale packed plenty of drama.

After two scoreless innings from both Max Fried, the Rays opened the scoring in the top of the third on an RBI single from Jonathan Aranda.

Ben Rice quickly answered back in the bottom half of the frame, however, with an RBI single of his own.

The back-and-forth scoring between the teams quickly became a theme.

Singles weren't necessarily a part of that theme, however, as Vilade snuck a homer over the short perch in right field in the top of the fourth:

Again the Yankees responded immediately and tied the game, this time courtesy of Spencer Jones.

But the Rays seized the lead back in the top of the top—and chased Max Fried out of the game in the process—with a no-doubter to right field from Victor Mesa Jr. to give the Rays a 4-2 lead.

You'll never guess what happened in the bottom of the sixth.

This time the Yankees didn't tie the game, though they came close, as Volpe's double to left field—initially ruled a homer before replay showed clear fan interference—cut the deficit in half.

"After viewing all relevant angles, the Replay Official definitively determined the spectator interfered with the ball over the field of play," MLB said in a statement . "The ball would not have left the playing field nor would it have been caught. The call is overturned, there was spectator interference and no home run. Additionally, the Replay Official scored one run and placed the batter-runner at second."

The Yankees still had three innings to erase the deficit from there but couldn't solve Tampa's bullpen, ending their season.

The Rays will now await either the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. The White Sox currently lead that series 2-1.

As for the Yankees, the attention now turns to the offseason and re-tooling a roster that simply couldn't will the Yankees further in the playoffs without the injured Aaron Judge. A few folks in the Big Apple will probably have some thoughts on what the Yankees should do this winter.

articles.title: Former MLB pitcher Roger Clemens to receive Medal of Freedom, Trump says
articles.summary: President Trump said he will award controversial baseball legend Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying the honor is a “big step up” from the MLB’s Hall of Fame — which has repeatedly declined to recognize him. “I’m pleased to announce that we are taking it into our own hands. Forget about the Hall…
articles.body:
President Trump said he will award controversial baseball legend Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying the honor is a “big step up” from the MLB’s Hall of Fame — which has repeatedly declined to recognize him.

“I’m pleased to announce that we are taking it into our own hands. Forget about the Hall of Fame; he’ll get there someday. I mean, I don’t know how they can keep him out,” Trump said before announcing Clemens’ Medal of Freedom recognition — the U.S.’s highest civilian honor .

Clemens, a Texas-raised former MLB player who ranks among the league’s most decorated pitchers, introduced the president at the start of the San Antonio event — aiming to boost Lone Star State GOP candidates less than a month before November’s elections.

He heaped praise on Trump, calling him a “man that loves our country” and calling on attendees to remember that “he put his life on the line for us.”

The baseball star of over 20 years was the subject of a federal probe surrounding his testimony to Congress about his 2008 performance-enhancing drug use allegations, according to Reuters . He was acquitted of related perjury charges in 2012.

Trump called on the Baseball Hall of Fame Committee in December to induct Clemens, blaming former President Obama’s Justice Department for what he described as using “rumors and innuendo” surrounding the alleged doping to inform its investigation.

“Roger Clemens is the only pitcher who has won 300 games to not have the honor of being enshrined in the Hall of Fame, which is a total travesty!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time. “He never tested positive and, when the Obama DOJ went after him in a criminal case claiming that he did take steroids, Roger, who has always denied taking any drugs, was FULLY ACQUITTED OF ALL CHARGES.”

Clemens took the stage to thank the president after he announced the award, calling the recognition a “huge honor” and joking that Trump had inflated his statistics in earlier remarks.

“There wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from,” the former pitcher, nicknamed “Rocket,” said.

articles.title: Rays sweep Yankees out of AL Division Series, extending New York’s title drought to 17 years
articles.summary: After sweeping Boston in the Wild Card Series, New York never led against the Rays and hasn’t advanced past a higher-seeded team in the postseason since 2020.
articles.body: Max Fried gave up two home runs, the New York Yankees had one taken off the board by fan interference and then their season ended Thursday night with a whimper. After Anthony Volpe’s would-be tying homer in the bottom of the sixth inning turned into a double on video review, the Yankees did not get a runner past second base. When leadoff hitter Trent Grisham struck out to end the ninth, it capped a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the AL Division Series and a series sweep that extended the Yankees’ championship drought to 17 years. After sweeping Boston in the Wild Card Series, New York never led against the Rays and has not advanced past a higher-seeded team in the postseason since 2020. Without injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Yankees were one-hit and shut out in the opener, when catcher Austin Wells’ baserunning blunder loomed large. Game 2 included four errors to get pushed to the brink of elimination. The Yankees didn’t go quietly — at least initially. When Fried gave up a run apiece in the third and fourth innings, the bats responded each time to tie the score. Victor Mesa Jr. crushed Fried’s 80th and final pitch for a go-ahead, two-run home run that was far from a short-porch homer like Ryan Vilade’s earlier. It looked like New York would get it right back in a redemption moment for Volpe, but a Jeffrey Maier-esque moment came back to haunt the home team 30 years later. With rookie George Lombard Jr. on base — and Wells would have been if not for a successful ABS challenge by the Rays — Volpe turned on right-hander Griffin Jax’s 95.9 mph sinker and hit it 357 feet to left field. It was a matter of inches as to whether a fan reached over the fence and interfered with the ball or it would have cleared the wall entirely. Although umpires on the field called it a home run, video review determined the fan did interfere. The replay official scored it an RBI double for Volpe with a run scored, but the run that did not turn out to be the difference. With the air sucked out of Yankee Stadium, Spencer Jones — who singled and doubled in his first two plate appearances — struck out swinging to end the threat. The eighth started with Paul Goldschmidt reaching on a throwing error and finished with fellow pinch-hitter Giancarlo Stanton striking out in just his second at-bat of the postseason. Stanton got chances to swing the bat after strained calf muscles in each of his legs sidelined him since April 24. Judge was not afforded the same opportunity, left off the rosters for the AL Wild Card Series and the ALDS because of his calf injury. The Yankees hit .130 in the series and were outscored 10-5. Aaron Boone again fell short of a title in his ninth season as New York’s manager, and some fans chanted “Fire Boone!” as they streamed to the exits.

articles.title: Dodgers beat Braves 4-1 to clinch NL Division Series after Pages’ go-ahead single in the 7th
articles.summary: The Dodgers advanced to the National League Championship Series as they seek to become the first NL team to win three straight World Series.
articles.body: ATLANTA — Andy Pages drove in two runs with a bases-loaded single in the seventh inning to give Los Angeles the lead, and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 4-1 on Wednesday night to clinch their NL Division Series. The Dodgers won back-to-back games in Atlanta to take the best-of-five matchup 3-1 and advance to the National League Championship Series as they seek to become the first NL team to win three straight World Series. Pages lined a 3-2 pitch from Robert Suarez up the middle to drive in Teoscar Hernández, who singled off starter Tyler Mahle, and pinch runner Tommy Edman for a 3-1 lead. Didier Fuentes walked pinch hitter Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases. Edman ran for De Paula. Max Muncy’s solo shot off Raisel Iglesias in the ninth padded the lead and gave the slugger 19 postseason homers with the Dodgers, extending his franchise record. Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow, making his first start since Sept. 24, allowed only one hit but walked five batters in 4 2/3 innings. After he issued two walks in the fifth, left-hander Alex Vesia ended the inning on Matt Olson’s groundout to second base. The missed opportunity left the Braves with 18 walks in the series, and none scored. Glasnow and four relievers combined to give up just three hits. Tanner Scott pitched a perfect eighth before Edwin Díaz got three quick outs for the save. Mahle, a native of Newport Beach, California, who grew up a Dodgers fan, allowed two runs — one earned — in 6 1/3 innings. Michael Harris II hit Glasnow’s first pitch for a single before stealing second and eventually scoring from third on a wild pitch that bounced off catcher Will Smith’s chest protector. The Dodgers pulled even in the second with the help of two Atlanta errors. Shohei Ohtani walked, stole second and advanced to third on catcher Sean Murphy’s errant throw into center field. Muncy’s pop fly into shallow left field was dropped by shortstop Mauricio Dubón for another error, allowing Ohtani to score. Hernández crashed into the wall while attempting to catch Ozzie Albies’ double off Vesia leading off the sixth. Hernández pointed to his head and neck when talking to an athletic trainer but remained in the game. Edgardo Henriquez stranded Albies at second. Henriquez allowed one hit in 1 2/3 scoreless innings for the win. Injury report Dodgers second baseman Miguel Rojas was held out after leaving Tuesday night’s 3-1 win during an at-bat in the eighth inning with lower back soreness. Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts said Rojas would not be available off the bench. Ronald Acuña Jr. started in right field for Atlanta one day after being moved to designated hitter in a late lineup change due to right knee soreness. He won't be getting much sympathy from Yankees' fans, however—Boone is not a popular man in the Big Apple at the moment:

"Those are conversations for another day," Boone told reporters Wednesday night when asked about his job security, which might be true for himself but certainly wasn't true among Yankees' fans.

In his nine seasons as Yankees' manager the team has yet to win a World Series title and only played in the Fall Classic once (2024). The Bronx Bombers have made the playoffs in eight of Boone's nine seasons but only advanced past the ALDS three times.

In some markets, that level of consistency would represent a memorable period. But given the Yankees' historical pedigree—and astronomical payroll, even if it no longer tops the sport—expectations are much higher.

At this point, Yankees' fans don't seem inclined to give Boone the benefit of the doubt despite the team being without injured superstar Aaron Judge. It's hard to imagine that general manager Brian Cashman will escape their wrath either. Yankees' fans are ready for the organization's 17-year title drought to end.

Whether ownership also fixates on the manager and general manager as the main culprit in that regard remains to be seen.

articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers will face each other in the National League Championship Series for the second straight year.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers will face each other in the National League Championship Series for the second straight year.

Each team closed out its respective Division Series on Wednesday with Los Angeles defeating the Atlanta Braves in four games and Milwaukee outlasting the San Diego Padres in four games. Now the top two seeds will face each other for a spot in the World Series.

Here is a look at some of the early information ahead of the NLCS rematch.

It's not going to be as easy this time for the Dodgers.

The two-time reigning World Series champions cruised to a four-game sweep of the Brewers in last year's series, but Milwaukee figures to pose a much more significant challenge in its second chance.

After all, this team won 103 games this season with World-Series-or-bust expectations since around the middle of the year. While last year's squad was coming off back-to-back losses in the NL Wild Card round, there is no happy-to-be-here feeling around the 2026 version that was just one step away from the World Series.

The Brewers also have arguably the game's best pitcher and the likely NL Cy Young winner in Jacob Misiorowski leading the way.

The fireballer took a major step this season, improving his ERA from 4.36 to 1.80. He led the league with 252 strikeouts and figures to take the ball multiple times over the course of an extended series.

But he is just one star pitcher facing a team that is loaded with them.

Los Angeles' pitching depth will ultimately make the difference in this series, like it will all the way to a third straight championship. It may be frustrating for fans of other teams, but it is as daunting of a task as one could face in baseball going up against the Dodgers' arms in a playoff series.

Tarik Skubal is an ace. Yoshinobu Yamamoto is an ace. Blake Snell is a two-time Cy Young winner. And Tyler Glasnow is as overqualified of a No. 4 starter as one could possibly imagine.

Even if Misiorowski wins a couple of games in the series, the Dodgers are going to have the starting pitching advantage every other time the right-hander is not on the mound.

Yamamoto may even be the best postseason pitcher in this series, as he captured last year's World Series MVP and picked up right where he left off by allowing just one run and striking out 10 in seven innings of work in a Game 3 win over the Braves on Tuesday.

He will be there to take the ball when the Dodgers need a series-turning win, and they will reach the Fall Classic once again.

articles.summary: For the second consecutive year, the Milwaukee Brewers are headed to the National League Championship Series.
articles.body:
For the second consecutive year, the Milwaukee Brewers are headed to the National League Championship Series.

The Brewers punched their ticket to the NLCS with a 3-1 victory over the San Diego Padres in Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday night.

Here's a look at the updated postseason bracket:

The Padres had a chance to strike first on Wednesday, loading the bases with two outs in the bottom of the first inning.

Xander Bogaerts popped out to end the frame, though.

Milwaukee eventually took a 1-0 lead in the top of the third, as Garrett Mitchell's RBI single brought Sal Frelick home.

The Brewers' excitement was short-lived, as Fernando Tatis Jr. immediately responded with a solo home run in the bottom of the inning to tie the contest at 1-1.

Milwaukee jumped back in front two innings later, as Mitchell hit a leadoff triple in the fifth before he eventually crossed home plate with a single from Jackson Chourio.

The Brewers extended their lead to 3-1 in the top of the sixth due to Frelick's sacrifice fly.

While the Padres were unable to put a runner in scoring position in both the sixth and seventh inning, they had an opportunity to tie the game in the bottom of the eighth.

With a runner on first base and one out, Mitchell robbed Manny Machado of a game-tying home run with an impressive catch in center field.

San Diego couldn't pull off a rally in the bottom of the ninth, as Milwaukee ended up emerging victorious.

The Brewers finished with 10 hits as a team and were able to consistently put pressure on the Padres' pitchers despite ultimately going just 2-for-12 with runners in scoring position.

Meanwhile, San Diego recorded a mere three hits while striking out nine teams as a team.

The Brewers will now face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS for the second consecutive season.

articles.title: Brewers finish off Padres to set up repeat clash with Dodgers in NLCS
articles.summary: The Dodgers swept the Brewers in last year's NLCS. But this is a different team.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers will face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS again. They can only hope it goes better than last year.Milwaukee finished off the San Diego Padres on Wednesday, posting a 3-1 victory in Game 4 to end the season of what was the hottest team in baseball this time last week. The Brewers’ four-game series win sets up a rematch of the 2025 NLCS.The Dodgers swept that series on their way to a second straight World Series title.STRUCK HIM OUT!The @Brewers are going back to the NLCS!@MLBONFOX pic.twitter.com/gtFtgeugNP— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 8, 2026 Game 1 of this year’s NLCS is scheduled for Sunday in Milwaukee. The Brewers will be looking to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982 and are still in pursuit of the first title in franchise history. Their victory Wednesday at least broke a record streak of 12 straight postseason road games lost.The Brewers came short of a sweep 24 hours earlier but hardly looked bothered by getting taken to a fourth game. Starting pitcher Robert Gasser threw four innings, with his only blemish a Fernando Tatis Jr. homer. Then Aaron Ashby came in and threw three scoreless, hitless innings.With six outs to get, the Brewers brought in elite setup man Abner Uribe, and that wound up being the Padres' best chance to save their season. With a runner on first in a two-run game, Manny Machado hit the ball high and hard.But he didn't hit it hard enough to get it past the reach of Brewers center fielder Garrett Mitchell, who fought off the fingers of a Padres fan to rob Machado of a game-tying homer.GARRETT MITCHELL TAKES AWAY A GAME-TYING HOME RUN 🤯 pic.twitter.com/UVjEXP3VA7— MLB (@MLB) October 8, 2026 As for the offense, the Brewers just kept coming. The lineup didn't strike out until the seventh inning, when Padres All-Star closer Mason Miller entered the game. Single runs came in the third, fifth and sixth innings, each off a different bat. It's honestly a wonder the Brewers didn't score more, having left 10 runners on base with a 2-for-12 performance with runners in scoring position.There were no surprises from San Diego this time, outside of that homer from Tatis, and now their season is over. Once again, it's a frustrating end for a Padres team that has spent like a contender for years, with just one unsuccessful trip to the NLCS to show for it. They Padres entered this series having won 19 of their previous 22 games, but two frustrating games in Milwaukee stopped that momentum cold.With Michael King, Robbie Ray, Adrian Morejon, Jason Adam and several others able to hit free agency this winter, it could be an expensive offseason for San Diego just to maintain this year's team. And with new ownership aboard, there's no telling what direction the franchise will go as MLB enters its own highly uncertain offseason.

articles.title: Impending free agent Jazz Chisholm Jr. hopes to be back with Yankees; Paul Goldschmidt not ready to call quits on career
articles.summary: Following a disappointing end to their 2026 season, the Yankees will take some time to reflect on what went wrong before eventually gearing up for another of...
articles.body:
Following a disappointing end to their 2026 season, the Yankees will take some time to reflect on what went wrong before eventually gearing up for another year to try and win a World Series.

Part of that preparation will come in the form of free agency, where New York will decide which players it wants to add or possibly run back for another go-around. In fact, the Yankees will have to make decisions on a few guys this offseason as players like Jazz Chisholm Jr. , Paul Goldschmidt and Trent Grisham will all become free agents.

For Chisholm and Grisham, it will be their first time on the open market while the veteran Goldschmidt has been in this position before.

"I do hope to be back," Chisholm said. "... This is where I want to be."

The 28-year-old who joined the Yanks at the 2024 MLB Trade Deadline has had an up-and-down tenure in New York. Chisholm got off to a great start after being acquired and hit 11 home runs in 46 games – power he hadn't exactly tapped into with the Miami Marlins – while playing third base, a position he was unfamiliar with but willing to play.

Chisholm fizzled offensively in the playoffs during the Yankees' World Series run, but he returned in 2025 and had a career year with 31 home runs, 80 RBI and a 4.1 WAR to go along with 31 steals after 40 (18 with New York) the season prior.

After another no-show in the playoffs, Chisholm returned to the Yankees on a one-year, $10.2 million contract to avoid arbitration, but for the first time in New York, found some struggles.

A disappointing season bled into a disappointing postseason, which culminated with manager Aaron Boone going with Anthony Volpe at second base over Chisholm in Game 3 against the Tampa Bay Rays to try and spark his offense -- a decision that Chisholm had "no comment" on following the loss.

"You guys thought I had a great year last year and I didn't even feel like I had a great year. It was a decent year, but [I] definitely didn't have my best year this year," Chisholm said.

Still, the versatile infielder who can also play the outfield, including center field, expressed his adoration for playing in New York and wants to stay put, although he knows there's a chance his days with the Yanks are done.

"I love it as a Yankee," he said. "I grew up as a Yankee fan. Being from the Bahamas, watching Derek Jeter and those guys every day. It was a great time being a Yankee, I love my time as a Yankee, I had great years with the Yankees, had an All-Star year, had a Silver Slugger year; it was great.

"I mean who doesn't want to stay with the team that you've had such great times with and great years with? To see it maybe end here sucks, but it's part of the business."

Another player New York might let go is Goldschmidt, who had a resurgence this season as the team's platoon first baseman a season after being the full-time first baseman in his first season with the Yanks.

Goldschmidt, now 39 years old, slashed .252/.313/.452 with 18 home runs in 345 at-bats and expressed his desire to keep playing next season. Whether that's with the Yankees, somewhere else or at all will be determined during the offseason.

"I'd like to continue playing so we'll see if that opportunity happens," Goldschmidt said. "I had a lot of fun playing here and just wanted to enjoy playing and enjoy competing and try to be part of and impact a team and help us win and was able to do that somewhat, but not ultimately get us with the group of guys here to win.

"So my mindset really hasn't changed, hopefully be able to have a chance to do that again and hopefully win a championship."

During his 16-year career, the seven-time All-Star, four-time Gold Glove winner, five-time Silver Slugger and 2022 MVP has never won a World Series.

As for Grisham, who accepted his qualifying offer last offseason for $22 million to be the Yankees' everyday center fielder, he regressed heavily after a career year in 2025.

Boone gave him an opportunity to get things started in Game 3 of the ALDS by moving him up to the leadoff spot, but Grisham finished 0-for-5 and made the final out of the game on a strikeout, which ended New York's season.

"The only thing I can say on it is I love the people here," Grisham said about his pending free agency. "I've loved playing here. It's a joy to show up every day and pull on the same side of the rope and really go after winning every day. I've loved my time here."
